author: 0xacb
text:
Just reproduced sshole (CVE-2026-123158), beautifully simple bug by @kultekin

Needs password auth on and no PAM, but you can ssh as root into an unpatched Alpine box with any 257+ byte password.

musl crypt() returns "*" for any password over 256 bytes. a locked account's shadow field is also "*". sshd compares them and they match.

fix: openssh 10.6p2

I was reading a blog on the "AI RCEssion" today, and it captures what happened during October: AI isn't creating new bugs, it's just auditing 10-to-20-year-old tech debt faster than manual teams can keep up.

Adversaries have automated their auditing, which means defenders must do the same.

That's why we built Zero, @Ethiack's public record of emerging 0-days. It tracks the earliest public signals of new vulnerabilities so you can validate real exploitability before attackers win the race.

author: 0xacb
text:
Attackers often exploit new vulnerabilities before defenders can react, sometimes before the vulnerability even gets a public ID (a CVE).

In the first half of 2026, 487 vulnerabilities were listed as exploited. For 137 of them (>25%), the exploitation record existed on or before the day the CVE was published.

We built Ethiack Zero to track emerging vulnerabilities from the first public signal (a patch, a GitHub advisory, news, a blog post) and validate actual exploitability before the CVE is officially published.

author: 0xiczc
text:
1/ Recently, I discovered a vulnerability in the  @0xPolygon zkEVM and earned my first L2 bug bounty from @Immunefi.
This vulnerability causes the assets being bridged from the L1 to Polygon zkEVM(L2) cannot be claimed properly in the L2, thus blocking L1->L2 asset migration.

author: 0xiczc
text:
2/ As we know, when a new user wants to use a rollup, they first need to bridge their L1 assets to L2.

In Polygon zkEVM, the technical workflow for this is implemented as follows:

author: 0xiczc
text: 3/ The user calls L1 SC bridgeAsset() to lock the asset. The bridge SC appends corresponding metadata to L1 Exit Tree, and updates L1 Exit Tree Root and Global Exit Tree Root in the SC. Afterward, the off-chain infra will sync the Global Exit Root from L1 to L2. [pic.x.com/MrvXQgcnsu]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FxDudwragAAlAjQ.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: 0xiczc
text: 4/ Once the root has been synced, any user can call L2 SC claimAsset() with Merkle proof and leaf index (deposit count) to demonstrate the correct exit leaf inclusion and mint an equivalent value representative asset to the recipient on L2.

author: 0xiczc
text:
5/ I noticed that the claim tx is designed to be free in the L2 node, which means that the gas price is allowed to be 0. Perhaps this is because new L2 users do not have ETH to pay the gas fee.

https://github.com/0xPolygonHermez/zkevm-node/blob/v0.0.6/pool/transaction.go#L55

https://github.com/0xPolygonHermez/zkevm-node/blob/v0.0.6/pool/pool.go#L346-L353 [pic.x.com/ZUYaDBa2BM]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FxDueYKaIAAvWD9.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: 0xiczc
text: 6/ I realized that malicious actors can send invalid free claim tx without any L1 deposit, but this is not possible in reality. To prevent the DoS attack, before the claim tx is added to the tx pool, the claim tx gets pre-executed to ensure that it will succeed.

author: 0xiczc
text:
7/ If duplicate claim tx are sent to the tx pool at the same time, they will both be pre-executed successfully under the same state.
To ensure that only one free claim is accepted for each L1 deposit, the claim tx added to tx pool will be marked as used with the deposit count.

author: 0xiczc
text:
8/ So far so good, but I believe that vulnerabilities may be hidden in the complexity and diversity introduced by this particular treatment of claim tx. Finally, I found an oddity in the code logic of handling claim tx pre-execution results.
https://github.com/0xPolygonHermez/zkevm-node/blob/v0.0.6/pool/pool.go#L182-L229

author: 0xiczc
text: 9/ Let's take a closer look at the snippet of code. If the claim tx is free (meaning gas price is equal to 0), and is reverted then return a `free claim reverted` error and isn't added to the tx pool. Otherwise, the deposit count is marked, and the tx is added to the tx pool.

author: 0xiczc
text: 10/ It seems fine at first glance, but upon thinking deeper, they forget that users can send non-free claim tx. It means the else statement (https://github.com/0xPolygonHermez/zkevm-node/blob/v0.0.6/pool/pool.go#L189) here actually contains three cases: free and non-revert, non-free and non-revert, and non-free and revert.

author: 0xiczc
text:
11/ The first two cases have the correct handling, but the third case incorrectly marks the revert claim tx deposit count and adds it to the tx pool regardless.
This breaks the expected design: the claim tx added to the tx pool must ensure successful execution.

author: 0xiczc
text: 12/ Therefore, we can bypass the `isReverted` pre-executed check of claim tx by setting the gas fee to non-zero(e.g., 1), this enables malicious actors to DoS the sequencer and prover by sending a large number of low-cost claim tx, thus increasing computational overhead.

author: 0xiczc
text: 13/ Furthermore, the tx is not deleted from the pool immediately after execution. The status is updated from "pending" to "selected" and continues to exist in the PostgreSQL DB. Currently, only one trusted sequencer is able to fetch transactions from the tx pool and execute them. [pic.x.com/431doxTOHq]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FxDugBpakAAZZ2U.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: 0xiczc
text: 14/ Thus another exploit is maliciously marking any deposit count by sending a failed tx. This causes the claim tx that correctly uses the deposit count to be rejected because the deposit count is already used. This makes the L2 network unusable for new users.

author: 0xiczc
text:
15/ The Polygon zkEVM team fixed this vulnerability by removing the particular gas logic for claim tx.
https://github.com/0xPolygonHermez/zkevm-node/pull/2048
Although no funds are at risk due to node upgradability, I think it is an interesting issue arising from the mix of contract and blockchain node logic.

someone will find the big, protocol wrecking, critical bug

capital flight and brand destruction happens overnight

entire savings lost, lives ruined financially, lawsuits filed, death threats received

i've seen it happen time and time again and it will happen to YOU if this is your approach to building on the blockchain

riptide's recommendations:

1) find a balance between securing the code and shipping fast. the security strategy should not be to push critical fixes like OTA updates for an XBOX game when any significant TVL is at risk.

2) invest in top tier human security talent. AI + expert SRs are a force multiplier. get a team that builds with a security first mindset from day 1.

3) properly incentivize responsible disclosure and treat your whitehats like kings. they are your last defense and will go out of their way to ensure your success if treated well

remember that you may only get one shot at building a successful project that makes you millions of dollars ...

best of luck anon

author: 0xteddav
text:
GKR is simple in spirit: verify a circuit layer by layer.
You start at the output.
Use Sumcheck to verify it's consistent with the layer below.
Then recurse.
Keep doing this until you reach the inputs.

author: 0xteddav
text:
Learning ZK and writing your first circuits?
It’s easy to make mistakes and introduce soundness bugs 🐞
To help you out, I walk you through some buggy Halo2 circuits (👋 @Zcash  @PrivacyScaling ) and show how to fix them step by step! 🧵 https://github.com/teddav/halo2-soundness-bugs

author: 0xteddav
text: 🧩 ZK circuits are all about constraints: you prove something is true without revealing it, as long as your circuit is sound. But it's way too easy to write insecure circuits 😅 Forget just one constraint and 💥 the prover can cheat and produce a valid proof for something false

author: 0xteddav
text:
The main part of the project is a Merkle tree circuit.
You prove a leaf belongs to a tree, but the prover can pass fake leaves. I walk through several buggy versions and explain why each one fails, until the circuit is finally sound 💪

https://github.com/teddav/tdd.nr

(7/12) https://twitter.com/decaylessfi/status/1906265780057972854

quoted.text:

SIR has been hacked, do not deposit any further funds.

We will post more asap.

author: ChainLight_io
text:
6️⃣ @leveragesir Loses $354K

• To bypass the checks, the exploiter bruteforced the vanity address by create2, and set the amount variable the same as the address.
• After that, exploiter called its malicious contract by callback and drained the assets.

(8/12) https://twitter.com/DecurityHQ/status/1906270316935942350

quoted.text:
Synthetics Implemented Right @leveragesir has been hacked for $355k

This is a clever attack. In the vulnerable contract Vault (https://etherscan.io/address/0xb91ae2c8365fd45030aba84a4666c4db074e53e7) there is a uniswapV3SwapCallback function that uses transient storage to verify the caller. Specifically, it loads an address of a Uniswap pool from the slot 0x1 and checks that it matches msg.sender. It looks right at the first glance, however at the end of the execution uniswapV3SwapCallback stores the value of the variable amount at the same slot!

Since the value of amount can be controlled externally, one has to find such an amount that will point to a controllable address. So did the hacker: they bruteforced a vanity address 0x00000000001271551295307acc16ba1e7e0d4281 (amount=95759995883742311247042417521410689) and provided precise arguments to mint exactly this number of tokens. After that they directed the flow of the execution such that this amount is stored at the slot 0x1 to replace Uniswap pool address and called uniswapV3SwapCallback from the bruteforced contract deployed with CREATE2 to drain the Vault (https://etherscan.io/address/0xb91ae2c8365fd45030aba84a4666c4db074e53e7). 

Attack tx: https://app.blocksec.com/explorer/tx/eth/0xa05f047ddfdad9126624c4496b5d4a59f961ee7c091e7b4e38cee86f1335736f

author: ChainLight_io

1️⃣ @zothdotio Loses $8.4M

• Due to the control hijacking exploit, proxy contract was upgraded to exploiter's malicious contract.
• The exploiter withdrew the entire USD0++ in the victim contract and swapped to DAI.
• Exploited assets have not moved since the exploit.

(3/6) https://twitter.com/zothdotio/status/1903447852418035986

quoted.text:
Security Incident Update –

Zoth Protocol experienced a targeted exploit through a malicious proxy upgrade. The attacker after multiple failed attempts gained unauthorized access to the deployer account and used it to upgrade the protocol to a malicious contract, enabling the unauthorized withdrawal of funds from a Segregated Vault holding USD0++ as Collateral.

On-chain activity shows that this was an orchestrated attack, with the attacker funding wallets and deploying contracts weeks in advance with multiple failed attempts before they succeeded yesterday. Post-exploit, funds were quickly moved and swapped to DAI and later ETH.

Currently, the funds are sitting in 0x7b0cd0D83565aDbB57585d0265b7D15d6D9f60cf

The team is actively investigating the incident and coordinating with professional experts to trace the stolen funds and recover them. In addition to that we have onboarded Crystal Blockchain BV to investigate the whole incident.

73% of the TVL on the Zoth platform has been secured immediately with the help of our Asset Issuer partners. We’re committed to full transparency and will continue to share updates as we uncover more details.

Through the help of our partners, we will be sharing the detailed report once we have the complete details in the coming weeks.

We appreciate the community, partners, and backers' support and patience during this time.

We have already announced a total public bounty of $500,000. Any actionable help in leading to fund recovery will be rewarded from the bounty.

— Team Zoth

author: Guhu95
text:
Glamsterdam upgrade contest rules wish-list🤞:
- POCs on-request only if needed.
- $750K pot: 50k infos, 250k lows, 450k meds + highs.
- Unconditional pot. No "Mythical Critical".
- No custom severity rules: regular platform rules with clarifications on how network safety and liveness impacts are treated.
- Judging authority remains with platform judges.
- Escalations open to everyone (for their own issues).
- Live fixes are announced in a special thread.
- No multipliers for early submissions.

Why this is better for Ethereum's security?

- Requiring POCs for all issues wastes a huge amount of very scarce time on things like vibe-fighting the different compilers, kurtosis quirks, writing and debugging scripts, and any number of tasks. Instead POCs can be requested by client team or judge IF it's actually needed. The impact from this change will be huge: 1.5x - 2x more time to find bugs.

- Pot size. The contest is a huge challenge, 10x-30x harder than the typical contest, especially for SRs new to this scope. EV should be attractive to compensate. 1M unconditional would be best, but 750K should be possible given the value delivered by past contests. 1.5x to EV

- Conditionals reduce perceived EV. Hated by many if not most SRs at this point. Also, since Highs were found in both, this was highly ineffective in Pectra and Fusaka - same money paid for less eyes. At least 1.5x perceived EV increase here.

- Bigger "Lows" pot: Pectra 250k lows pot was a great EV signal and was also inclusive of more impacts. Fusaka's 25k infos pot was a terrible collective rug (80+ unique fixed issues for 25k in total + no dups). Impact: 2x EV.

- Broader severity rules: narrow scope rules caused a lot of frustration, escalations, discussions, delays, and general pain for everyone. Custom severity rules are a huge known "red-flag" for contests. Too many issues became "infos", in a way that's incompatible with future participation under similar rules. Some great SRs found "only" infos when judging was done - they will never return for a similar treatment unless rules are different. 2x EV increase from this.

- Judgement should be left to the hosting platform. In general, "sponsor judging" is a huge red-flag. Judging requires a lot of judging experience and a specific skill set - sponsors generally are not trusted by SRs to possess either, and are not impartial. In this contest a lot of seemingly in-scope findings were downgraded, and a lot of explicitly-OOS findings were upgraded. Note that making the pot unconditional makes this especially easy, since it makes the budget fixed. 30%-50% +EV due to more predictable judging.

- Escalations should be open to everyone - like it was done by Sherlock for Fusaka🙌. Otherwise, most SRs that use other platforms, or don't do contests generally are looking at a huge reduction of EV. 2x EV increase from announcing this ahead of time.

- Looking for fixes independently is a terrible waste of time. Each client repo has tens or hundreds of recently active or open PRs or branches, which can contain a fix anywhere. Reviewing these additional hundreds of diffs daily is a huge waste of time. Not reviewing them saves time, but leads to disappointment. Client teams can report contest-related fixes to the judges, who can post it to a common thread - this would save 90% of the pain. 10%-20% participation increase from saved time.

- Multipliers. Whoever can start early - will start early, to have more time available, and to benefit from "live fixes" policy which already creates a huge incentive to be early. So multiplers' positive effect adds nothing, but the negative effect of reducing EV for late joiners remains. Whoever can only join late, sees lower EV for doing so. 10-30% increase in EV by fixing this.

Of course, the effects don't add up linearly, and there is a fixed pool of SRs, and a fixed amount of time they can contribute. But these rules' goal is to make participating in Glam a "no brainer" good EV decision for SRs.

Hopefully, this can help us achieve even better security for future upgrades.

quoted.text:
Some Fusaka contest thoughts:

The Good:
- Client diversity still a mind boggling security super power.
- EF doing contests for upgrades is great for security, and sets the right example.
- AI is a game-changer, indispensable in huge complex scopes.
- Geth is still the Goat - more secure, more readable, and more correct than even the spec.
- @alexfilippov314 dominates again! Only 1 info finding is a crazy flex.

The Bad:
- Cryptography is still a bug hotspot.
- 2 KZG libraries for 11 clients is the Achilles heel of client diversity.
- PeerDAS is a whole new blockchain (a sharded one!) which is awkwardly entangled in the existing Ethereum chain. The surface area for severe issues is now much larger, even in parts that used to be non-critical.

The Ugly:
- Contest rules were even more impossible than for Pectra. The more frustrating a contest is, the less participation it gets. Less eyes -> less security. There were 950 submissions for Monad, and only 360 submissions for Ethereum - it should be the other way around.
- The upgrade did not go smoothly this time :(

A crazy ride and learning experience as always.

quoted.author: Guhu95
quoted.text:
You can measure how vulnerable the code is after a contest. This can help:
- Projects and users to estimate hack risk
- Bug hunters to scope targets
- Ecosystem to track what works best
- Platforms to manage reputation risk

TL;DR: More solo findings -> more hidden bugs.

This works for most formats: flat pot, conditionals, invitationals, reserved auditors. As long as duplicates are allowed.

### Recent examples: 

- Cork exploit: last private contest had 4 solo mediums (out of 4 total mediums). "Chao 1 bias-corrected" estimates 6 unfound bugs. Jackknife 8 more bugs.

- BeraBorrow's Recon's recent post about a critical: private contest had 8 solo mediums (out of 15 mediums), 6 doubletons (doubletons = found by two auditors). Chao 1: 4.5 more bugs, Jackknife: 9 more bugs.

### The science of capture-recapture

There are many disciplines that use this approach: software engineering, quality control, biology & ecology, epidemiology, criminology, linguistics. 

Similarly, there are many estimator formulas: Lincoln-Petersen, Chapman, Schnabel, Schumacher–Eschmeyer, Jolly–Seber, Chao 1 & 2, ACE, ICE, Jackknife 1 & 2, Bootstrap, Zelterman, Good–Turing, etc. Will post some links below.

Two simple examples are Jackknife 1 & 2, Chao 1 & 2 which roughly say :

- Jackknife 2 (second-order, simplified): `unfound = 2 * uniques - doubletons`. Jackknife is more popular in software-inspection studies.

- Chao 1: `unfound = (uniques^2) / (2 * doubletons)`. (A slightly different version for no doubletons)

Specifics don't matter really - pick your favorite from the long list. What's important is they all say: more unique findings -> more hidden bugs. 

### Intuitions

Math is not always intuitive, so here are some intuitions.

1. Parallel worlds: If a bug is unique to one finder, there’s a parallel world where it stayed hidden because he got sick, or was booked on an audit, or just missed it. Maybe you're in that parallel world. In contrast, if there are many duplicates - in most worlds the same bugs are found.

2. Serial auditing: If you imagine auditors working in sequence, the contest is just a stopping point for the sequence. The contest with uniques stopped when new bugs were still being found, so more like these remain. In contrast, the contest with only duplicates stopped after finding most bugs of similar rarity.

### What can we do?!

1. Measure: what platforms, pot sizes, contest formats give the best coverage?
2. Educate clients on the more secure formats with data.
3. If you're a project, check if your contest was weak.

### No solo findings = code is safe? No. 

It's possible whole classes of niche bugs (e.g. cryptography) or higher complexity bugs were not found because pot was too low. That's always a risk.

This rule doesn't tell as what's safe, but it tells us what's LIKELY still vulnerable.

---------

See next tweet for links and statistical nitpicking

author: Guhu95
text:
### Links
- https://blog.uvm.edu/tdonovan-vtcfwru/files/2020/06/18-Donov-pages-315-CB.pdf
- https://www.uvm.edu/~ngotelli/manuscriptpdfs/Chapter%204.pdf
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good%E2%80%93Turing_frequency_estimation

### Stats nitpicks

Directionally most nitpicks don't matter here, since "more uniques -> more hidden bugs" remains true. But:  

1. We assume mostly independent auditors, because of anti-sybil payout formula, and correlation causing underestimation (more duplicates) so is fine.

2. Doubletons vs. duplicates. Using any duplicates instead of doubletons is easier, but fine since underestimates.

3. If F2 (doubletons) is zero, Chao 1 as quoted doesn't work, so use something else, like the bias-corrected version.

4. Severity matters? Possibly, but also maybe not. Complexity (difficulty of finding) and its severity (impact and likelihood) are many times independent.

text:
Audit contests are just a spectator sport. That's the only sane way to treat them. Proof:

- Endless drama all the time.
- Top 0.1% are worshiped as demigods.
- Top 1% make more money from selling other stuff (audit days).
- Bottom 99% are there because of top 0.1%'s winnings.
- https://t.co/7LjPpRdsqh

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text:
Cross-model review still paid off for us on one thing: code that looks protected.

Two Opus review agents found guards in our bug-hunting pipeline that failed open. One matched against a term table nobody had filled. Empty table, everything passes.

That's where review still https://twitter.com/garrytan/status/2117661001332240434

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text:
Two of our agent tools had high failure rates. Same metric, opposite meanings.

One was a guardrail doing its job. The other was a broken tool eating our exploit runs. 🧵

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text:
Our file-search tool failed on about 1 call in 7.

Looked like a bug. It wasn't. Nearly every failure was a permission denial. The agents were hitting policy, which is what policy is for.

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text:
The test-network tool our exploit-writing agents use failed on more than 4 calls in 5.

Almost none were denials. They were real errors. The tool, not the agents, was burning most of our PoC attempts.

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text:
As models find more bugs, the hard part shifts to which findings you keep.

We tried 3 ways to make our detection agent report only bugs with a confirmed-live entry point. All 3 got reverted.

The gate threw out real findings along with the noise. https://twitter.com/OpenAI/status/2117444048227123277

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text:
LLMs are digging up bugs in decades-old Postgres code.

The flip side in node security: across 100+ fresh disclosures, the median age of the vulnerable code was under two months. Most were mismatches between parts written separately.

Old code hides bugs. New code makes them. https://twitter.com/lenny_enderle/status/2117177534039134253

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text: AI agents read a codebase in the order you list it. Put the critical file last and a bigger budget just buys a longer read of the wrong files. Scope order is part of the prompt.

author: GuplerSaxanoid
text: Our best AI-audit prompt change wasn't a checklist. It was one sentence about who wrote the code: everything the untrusted side exports is attacker-written, even the small helpers.

author: KeiZo_Zo
text:
AI doesn’t replace humans in bug hunting. It just promotes the human from ground-level manual work into more of a managerial, oversight, and guidance role ✨

What's your take on AI within bug bounties?

5/5

author: KeiZo_Zo
text:
That said, don’t get AI "led" bug bounty hunting wrong.
I put "led" in quotes because yes, AI does most of the heavy lifting, but humans still need to guide it to the right places with the right mindset. Once AI finds something, a human still needs to validate it rigorously
 
4/5

author: KeiZo_Zo
text:
This fact sticks out, when I tell you that out of the 27 valid findings, 12 of them were duplicates. 
Besides these duplicates, I still found my way to new findings and 8 paid reports demonstrate this clearly. Last 7 reports are still open

3/5

author: KeiZo_Zo
text:

However the numbers also show us that the AI is really being utilized by many of the bug bounty hunters 

2/5

author: Kiki_developer
text:
Maybe I’m out of the loop but what’s wrong with an unpaid internship? And how many better options are there?

- Contest are scarce and I don’t see that trend changing. 
- bounties can be a headache for those that are successful let alone people that are just starting out.  
- Contracting gigs without a network or portfolio are few and far between. 

Obviously if you can make any of the above three work then it’s a no brainer go do that. 

But if I started my career in 2026 instead of 2022 I would strongly consider an internship. The value of working through the entire lifecycle of an audit, learning from experienced auditors, building up a portfolio isn’t worthless. It’s actually pretty valuable

author: PwningEth
text:
The technical details have been explained by @immunefi . https://medium.com/immunefi/aurora-infinite-spend-bugfix-review-6m-payout-e635d24273d
Here is my short summary

author: PwningEth
text: 1/ The Aurora engine implements token bridging in prebuilt contracts at hardcoded addresses. They are the magical bridges connecting Ethereum, NEAR and Aurora.

author: PwningEth
text: 2/ The vulnerable contract always emits a fixed address in bridging events, assuming the msg.value will be collected by itself. However, if the contract is invoked by delegatecall(), the msg.value will never be sent to the contract but the log will be emitted as usual.

author: PwningEth
text: 3/ By repeating the malicious withdrawal then redeposit process, the attacker can double their balance exponentially. The infinity inflation of ETH could have destroyed the whole ecosystem of Aurora:

author: PwningEth
text: 4/ all 71k ETH in the aurora account could have been drained, and other valuable tokens could have been purchased by free ETH. (There were billions of TVL in the Aurora bridge.)

author: PwningEth
text: 5/ If you are hardcore enough, you may find the original report and scripts interesting https://app.ardrive.io/#/drives/7ba902d8-d26a-4dad-99b8-807eaaf8d925?name=AURORA , enjoy🤪!

author: PwningEth
text:
1/ Hey I’m pwning.eth! A few months ago, I reported a critical bug in the @auroraisnear Aurora Engine - a layer 2 EVM solution built for the @NEARProtocol. The catch got me a $6M payout, the 2nd highest payout in history!
Here’s some background,

author: PwningEth
text: 2/ Been watching the hacking drama in the crypto world for a while, and what a wild wild west it is! I’m a top-tier vulnerability researcher from Web2 and didn’t pay too much attention to Web3 until the story of @saurik (Optimism bug), he’s super famous in the jailbreak community

author: PwningEth
text: 3/ Now regarding how I started on Aurora, I’d say it’s pretty lucky. I checked the bounty list on @immunefi , and saw it offered a huge bounty 🤩.

author: PwningEth
text: 4/ The system seems to be solidly built for finding common exploits, but it’s complex enough that I smell chances of maybe more sophisticated attacks, so I thought “let’s capture the flag!”

author: PwningEth
text: 5/ I have pwned many more advanced complex systems in the real world, I know where the blindspot is. Once I started looking at the engine, I saw the unicorn bug after only a few hours of digging around.

author: PwningEth
text: 6/ 70,000 ETH can be hacked! ($200M+ at the time 😱😱😱, now ~$70M i guess 😆), would have been in the top 5 heists in DeFi’s history.

author: PwningEth
text: 7/ In quite a shock (after all $200M are hackable…), I spent some time verifying and reproducing the bug just in case it was a false alarm. Took me a few more days to test and finally finished the bug report

author: PwningEth
text: 8/ Pinged the Aurora team in discord and sent the report through Immunefi. They confirmed and patched the vulnerability super quickly and invited me to a video chat and cheered for me! These guys are really good, honest and responsive!

author: PwningEth
text: 9/So there you go, $6M 🤠🤠🤠… Honestly, it’s just crazy everything that’s going on in Web3. I’m super excited to start my own journey here, stay tuned 🥳!

author: Rhynorater
text: Here are a couple alternative bug bounty goals you could consider setting this year instead of the typical "I wanna earn X".

author: Rhynorater
text:
Vuln Types
Example: "I'd like to find 3 authentication bypasses in 2024"

This puts emphasis on progressing as a hacker and becoming proficient in other vulnerability types.

author: Rhynorater
text:
Systemization goals
Example: "I'd like to automate finding new endpoints pushed to XYZ .js file because they have a high chance of being vuln."

Thinking about how you can convert current bug bounty success into a system(technically automated or not) will help continuous success.

author: Rhynorater
text:
Research Goals
Example: "I'd like to identify 1 systemic issues in XYZ technology or stack that was previously unknown."

Doing original research is a kickass way of earning bounties - especially when you've got an automation system (or a @naglinagli) who fully exploit it.

text:
* There are ALWAYS critical
No matter how hardened a scope is, there is some hacker that can find a critical. Keep your eyes on high value bugs, and you might be the one who does.

* When unfamiliar with a company's threat model, report everything

text: After ramping up my hacking and completing the aforementioned bugs, I'd expect my bugs per month to increase to around 7 at $750 per bug, putting me at $5,250 with the 40/60 split mentioned above. That's roughly 80 hours over the month. Or one bug every 10 or so hours.

author: Rhynorater
text:
After months 4&5, at the above allocation, I'd be finding at least 12 bugs at $750 - $1k per bug (I'm getting better at finding impactful bugs - my current average bounty is $1.8k). 

This will put me at ~ 9k a month starting from month 6. Having earned 15.5k already this year.

author: Rhynorater
text:
Months 8-12 would be 100% hacking finding 15-20 bugs per month at 1k each.

So, if my calculations are correct, that would put me at:
17.5*1000*4 + 9000*2 + 5250*2 +2250*2 = $103,000

In reality, that number would likely be closer to $90,000 because of dupes and bounty flux.

text:

author: S1r1u5_
text:
fr tho, the <10k follower CTF/bug bounty/security research bubble was so much fun. i used to tweet all kinds of crazy shit, and people used to think i was either one-shotted or on drugs all the time(never did xd).

it was all fun banter, people would disagree, call out my takes with constructive critcism, and we would laugh about it at conferences. i probably said even more ridiculous shit in person.

but ig at some point, once you cross a certain follower count, you can't just shitpost freely anymore. you have to be more careful about how you phrase things because everything gets taken seriously or interpreted in the worst possible way. and idk, it feels like the discourse has gotten a bit more toxic lately or maybe it is what happens if small corner of internet gets bigger.

quoted.text:
Social media bubbles are not working anymore… 

How can I get back to my bubble with people who want to talk about vulnerability research, bug hunting, CTFs, fuzzing, reverse engineering, tooling, code review, …

And not constantly have to read: “You don’t know what you are talking about. Most companies don’t get hacked by vulnerabilities.”

You all think you are so smart and you figured it out… So it might come as a surprise 🙀 but I am well aware! It’s not rocket science. I am just not interested in it and I don’t have to be.

author: S1r1u5_
text:
apart from ip options potentially being dropped in transit, kernel text leaks taking time, and exploit reliability varying across configurations, for everyone to have peace of mine:

open models can't reliably exploit this vulnerability on its own without an experienced operator guiding it.

so you're all fine, php2shell is considerably easier to exploit than this, and even open models struggled with that. it is probably only openai and anthropic internal frontier models that can reliably pull this off autonomously :)

quoted.author: S1r1u5_
quoted.text:
regarding cve-2026-98432: it is a uaf in tcp, mptcp is needed to make the race win and to get the leak and write.

the impact of the bug is bad, its essentially go2shell, caddy2shell etc. go 1.24+ servers are all vulnerable, because mptcp  is enabled by default.

BUT:

1. It is extremely hard to win the race reliably, anthropic said it took 40 mins for them to get leak and defeat kaslr 
2. It is probably hard to exploit in practice. most routers, lbs and isps drop ip options, without that header you can't race at all, so realistically only a same network attacker can try, which is pretty common in sandbox infra

my mythos worked on this for last 3 days burned ~$2k and couldn't build a reliable poc that can be sprayable. gpt-5.6 sol als exhausted my subscription and couldn't even get a leak. 

either anthropic has a unreleased model which is better than their public one or they have a pro exploit dev internally.

author: WhiteHatMage
text:
Quick thoughts on the events I missed over the past two months:

- The XRP bug is a great finding, but the reward was low. But even Ethereum had a $250k max bounty a few months ago, so I wouldn’t criticize Ripple too hard.

- The max cap wasn’t specified in the XRP bounty program, so most hunters didn’t even bother checking it.

- The $50k Vercel bounty is too low. They advertised a $1 million bounty, which is misleading, since there's a $50k max cap. Are they expecting 20 Criticals?

- Other projects continue lowering their bounties or closing programs while hacks increase. I understand that it hurts to pay so many reports, but there’s no coming back from a hack.

- The “Duplicates” problem hasn’t been solved. You can still report a Critical issue, prevent major damage to a project and its users, and they will still try to find a way to pay you nothing while pointing to some non-impactful report as sharing the same root cause. Platforms should address this scam immediately.

- The LLM decompilation movement is pretty cool. It's the end of the era of closed-source code.

- People building security tools that depend on LLM tokens should try to make a profit today, or have a clear plan to sell their company before models get better. There's no long-term plan.

- LLM spam continues to be the main trend for getting bounty rewards. It feels like buying lottery tickets. The more tokens people spend, the more chances they have of landing an actual exploit. Having a unique approach seems to help too. But nobody is performing much better than the model they use, since there's no clear outstanding winner in the leaderboards.

- We’re getting to the end of 2026, and bounty rewards paid haven’t increased 10x with AI. According to Grok, for the top 100 on Immunefi the total earnings were:
* 2026 $16M, 1364 reports
* 2025 $11M, 820 reports
* 2024 $21M, 775 reports 
* 2023 $17M , 559 reports
* 2022 $57M, 443 reports

- What happened with Ledger is worrisome. Keep improving your OpSec, whitehats.

Personal thoughts:

We keep seeing more and more bugs in all kind of software. That's not because of superhuman AI capabilities. It's because how bad we've been building software over decades in terms of security.

Nobody cared about exploits because they were difficult for the average hackers. Now everyone has a low-level-IQ tool that can crack neglected code, and we see the results.

We're in a transition phase, where LLMs trained with human bugs are outperforming the average guys. We'll probably get to an era of LLMs-code-first, with LLM bugs that with unprecedented vulnerabilities.

Yes, LLMs are just that bad at coding, and the current models might not be able to see some obvious errors, since they also have "cognition bias".

I see a bright future for bounty hunters, full of vulnerabilities waiting to be found and prevented. We just need to solve the bug-pocalypse first if we don’t want blackhats to win.

author: _bagipro
text:
An attack on Android content providers that researchers might overlook

[1/4] Android has a mechanism to restrict access using the exported attribute or by requiring permissions

author: _bagipro
text:
[2/4] But system apps ("android.uid.system" and maybe systemui) automatically bypass these restrictions and can access arbitrary components
[3/4] It's trivial to force a system app to call ContentResolver.query() or openInputStream() for an arbitrary Uri

author: _bagipro
text: [4/4] If the implementation of ContentProvider.getType(), query(), openFile() does anything other than simply returning a ParcelFileDescriptor or data from a database (making directories, debug mode, dumping logs), an attacker can trigger it this way and gain privilege escalation

author: _bagipro
text:
New Android host validation bypass technique!

[1/4] All parsed URIs in Android are http://android.net.Uri.StringUri objects. However, the scheme parser only looks for the ":" delimiter [pic.x.com/IxCQxxP2gF]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GxR5F8GXsAAL0e-.jpg — no alt text provided by author
- photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GxR5F8rXYAInjnN.jpg — no alt text provided by author
- photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GxR5F8AXwAAfTxY.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: _bagipro
text: [2/4] You can insert slashes to bypass the host check like this: "bad_dot_com#/://good_dot_com". The default "http" scheme will be used

author: _bagipro
text: [3/4] This will only work if the scheme isn't validated either. This attack can increase the impact in cases when, e.g., the victim's access token is appended to the request headers

author: _bagipro
text:
[4/4] Limitations:
1. The lack of scheme validation
2. You also need to bypass the network security config:
- Easy case: usesCleartextTraffic is set to "true"
- Hard case: checking the app's network security config and trying to load your own host (or you control DNS responses)

author: _bagipro
text: [1/4] If you are looking for vulnerabilities in system apps on Android, pay attention to permissions. Very often they are used but not declared anywhere. This allows an attacker to declare and use them.

author: _bagipro
text: [2/4] In my experience, absolutely all vendors, including Google, are prone to this error. Moreover, the list of permissions and protected broadcasts is different for different devices of the same vendor.

author: _bagipro
text: [3/4] I've already described this bug in the article on permission errors in ecosystem apps (https://blog.oversecured.com/Common-mistakes-when-using-permissions-in-Android/#ecosystem-mistakes), but it turns out that Android vendors often don't do it right either.

author: _bagipro
text:
[4/4] If you have a physical device whose security you're researching, it's easy to check if permission is declared or not. All you need to do is run the command:

adb shell pm list permissions -f | grep com.permission

author: _bagipro
text:
When you test a mobile app for vulnerabilities, it's important to observe logs. There's a tip for Android apps.

[1/3]
App runtime logs:
adb logcat --pid=`adb shell pidof -s http://com.app.package`

Java crash logs:
adb logcat -s AndroidRuntime

author: _bagipro
text:
[2/3]
Native crashes:
adb logcat -s libc,DEBUG

author: _bagipro
text:
[3/3]
It could help you to detect a lot of things including:
- logging sensitive data such as network requests containing personal data and access tokens
- for obfuscated apps, it helps a lot to see how the app is executed and did you bypass a validation or not

author: _bagipro
text:
Bypassing ContentProvider.openFile() internal security checks in Android

[1/3]
I've discovered an interesting trick that you may use to access private information using a content provider [pic.x.com/xrljinxYO8]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FZaUqM4XkAIJZ7K.jpg — no alt text provided by author
- photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/FZaUrV0XwAYUPdc.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: _bagipro
text:
[2/3]
The attack is possible if:
1. The content provider is exported
2. Internally, it checks the calling UID, package name, and/or permission set as shown on the screenshots

author: _bagipro
text:
[3/3]
It's possible to call ContentProvider.openFile() via IActivityManager.openContentUri(). It will check access rights, but then proxy the call from its context leading to Binder.getCallingUid() == 1000, and all permissions granted

Regarding the recent attack on @injective, I want to make one thing very clear: this incident has absolutely nothing to do with me.

To this day, Injective still has not paid me any bug bounty. I am no longer arguing about this, and I have zero expectations from them anymore. For the past few months, I have been busy researching other things. I have received about $300,000 USD in total from bug bounties and audit contests.

I will use 10% of this money to expose their fraud. However, I have not decided how or when to spend this money yet. I do not plan to put too much of my time and energy into this right now. Because of this, the plan might be delayed for a very long time.

I am currently hunting bugs on @immunefi and @cantinasecurity . Thank you to all the projects that value security and integrity.

quoted.author: GoPlusSecurity
quoted.text:
1/4
⚠️ Exploit Breakdown: #Injective binary options settlement bug
On Sept 1, @Injective was exploited via a binary options settlement flaw and drained of ~$4.8M. The attacker bridged funds to Ethereum and swapped into$ETH:0x9137a6b20b083b07b84294d51ebc04a326787a2d

Triple-bug combo. Chain halted. Patch shipped.

1. Unbounded market_id string concat → ID collision. An INJ-denominated insurance fund could share the same market_id as a USDC binary options market.
https://github.com/InjectiveFoundation/injective-core/blob/b994d6b/injective-chain/modules/exchange/types/market.go#L52
https://github.com/InjectiveFoundation/injective-core/blob/b994d6b/injective-chain/modules/insurance/keeper/insurance.go#L398

2. Self-trades minted a fake settlement deficit. Attacker-controlled subaccounts crossed Long/Short orders against themselves to fabricate a non-existent funding gap.
https://github.com/InjectiveFoundation/injective-core/blob/5c3143ed621ed4e4a5d74d64ea952f5a8cda4c1f/injective-chain/modules/exchange/keeper/binaryoptions/market.go#L202-L226
https://github.com/InjectiveFoundation/injective-core/blob/5c3143ed621ed4e4a5d74d64ea952f5a8cda4c1f/injective-chain/modules/exchange/keeper/binaryoptions/market.go#L253-L264

3. Decimal mismatch. INJ wei (18 decimals) was compared directly against USDC (6 decimals), causing remainingDeficit to round to zero. The haircut was completely bypassed, and positions were refunded at full face value.
withdrawalAmount := absoluteDeficitAmount.Ceil().RoundInt() // USDC, 6 decimals
if http://insuranceFund.Balance.LT(withdrawalAmount) { ... }       // INJ base units, 18 decimals

4. Following the attack, Injective halted the chain and deployed a patch: https://github.com/InjectiveFoundation/injective-core/commit/b994d6b603eb53a38312e547f7bbe3c69d40495b
validateInsuranceFundDenom now strictly enforces that the insurance fund’s DepositDenom matches the market’s QuoteDenom across PayDeficitFromInsuranceFund, TransferFullInsuranceFundBalance, and MoveCoinsIntoInsuranceFund—effectively plugging the exploit vector.

This upgrade is a post-exploit fix. Not a coincidence.

author: al_f4lc0n
text:
the figures referenced in the post are entirely misleading. There was no impact realized from this issue. Zero user funds were affected and zero addresses were compromised.

My response: Are you suggesting I should have actually exploited the bug and caused real damage before coming to talk to you?

For the stated vulnerability to work in practice, it would require execution of several suspicious transactions that would have an extraordinarily limited impact.

My response: You should know better than anyone that on a Cosmos-based chain, a single transaction can pack multiple messages. Just one transaction is more than enough to completely drain multiple whale accounts.

Injective has dynamic rate limiting functionalities which are applied automatically based on our live monitoring systems. This functionality has been live on mainnet since last year and is publicly available in our code base.

My response: First, this has nothing to do with the vulnerability itself. Rate limiting doesn't stop attackers from stealing funds. It only slows them down when they try to bridge those funds over to Ethereum. Second, when I submitted my report, the mainnet configuration for this feature was not set. In other words, this feature wasn't even turned on!

In addition to all of the above, this report was reviewed against the clearly defined terms of our Immunefi program. Based on those terms, issues such as those raised in this report that DO NOT impact block production or consensus are categorized outside of the Blockchain/DLT tier and carry a maximum payout of $50,000.

My response: First, Immunefi has always put the impact of direct fund theft at the very top of its priority list. This is a fact that everyone knows. Second, you changed your bug bounty page after I submitted my report. Here’s the snapshot from November 8, 2025: https://web.archive.org/web/20251108165417/https://immunefi.com/bug-bounty/injective/information/ . And now, there’s an extra line added to your bug bounty page: “IMPORTANT: Within the Assets in Scope table, the injective-core folder is listed for both Blockchain/DLT and Web/App due to overlap between the two within the same folder. However, for a report to be categorized as Blockchain/DLT, the resulting impact has to be directly involved with the block production process or with consensus failures. All reports not dealing directly with either of these are to be categorized as Web/App.” I’d really like to know when this line was added. and do you really value chain consensus more than users' funds?

We remain committed to fair, transparent, and consistent handling of all reports, and to maintaining the highest standards of security for the ecosystem. Injective has done so since its mainnet inception in 2021 and will continue to do so in perpetuity, always putting builders and security first.

My response: You never even replied to my messages, and now you’re blaming me for not requesting mediation? I can post the original report if you agree. I left many messages, but you haven't replied to a single one.

----------

Finally: Stop making excuses from every angle and trying to use technical jargon to confuse people who aren't developers. That doesn’t work anymore these days. Anyone can just ask an AI to fact-check what both of us are saying. I have no ill intentions toward your project. All I'm asking is for you to be honest and handle this transparently.

quoted.text:
Security is paramount at @injective and we take our bug bounty program very seriously.

First and foremost, the figures referenced in the post are entirely misleading. There was no impact realized from this issue. Zero user funds were affected and zero addresses were compromised.

For the stated vulnerability to work in practice, it would require execution of several suspicious transactions that would have an extraordinarily limited impact. Injective has dynamic rate limiting functionalities which are applied automatically based on our live monitoring systems. This functionality has been live on mainnet since last year and is publicly available in our code base.

In addition to all of the above, this report was reviewed against the clearly defined terms of our Immunefi program. Based on those terms, issues such as those raised in this report that DO NOT impact block production or consensus are categorized outside of the Blockchain/DLT tier and carry a maximum payout of $50,000.

If the poster had requested a mediation we would explain to him the dynamic rate limiters and monitoring systems we have in place and why his stated figures are misleading. However, he did not do so. We always follow the procedures set forth by the Immunefi program and expect the submitter to do so as well.

We remain committed to fair, transparent, and consistent handling of all reports, and to maintaining the highest standards of security for the ecosystem. Injective has done so since its mainnet inception in 2021 and will continue to do so in perpetuity, always putting builders and security first.

author: al_f4lc0n
text:
I Saved Injective's $500M. They Pay Me $50K.

I like hunting bugs on @immunefi . I'm decent at it.

- #1 — Attackathon | Stacks
- #2 — Attackathon | Stacks II
- #1 — Attackathon | XRPL Lending Protocol
- 1 Critical and 1 High from bug bounties (not counting this one)

Life was good. Then I found a Critical vulnerability in @injective .

This vulnerability allowed any user to directly drain any  account on the chain. No special permissions needed. Over $500M in on-chain assets were at risk.

I reported it through Immunefi. The next day, a mainnet upgrade to fix the bug went to governance vote. The Injective team clearly understood the severity.

Then — silence. For 3 months. No follow up. No technical discussion. Nothing.

A few days ago, they notified me of their decision: $50K. The maximum payout for a Critical vulnerability in their bug bounty program is $500K. I disputed it. Silence again. No explanation for the reduced payout. No explanation for the 3 month ghost. No conversation at all. To be clear: the $50K has not been paid either.

I've seen others share bad experiences with bug bounty payouts recently.  I never thought it would happen to me. I can't force them to do the right thing. But I won't let this be forgotten.

I will dedicate 10% of all my future bug bounty earnings to making sure this story stays visible — until Injective pays what I deserve.

Full Technical Report: https://github.com/injective-wall-of-shame/bug-any-account-ordering/blob/main/report.md

text: $300k for a trusted internal header! I wonder if Param Miner found it... congrats to the discoverer either way! https://twitter.com/dps/status/2117451520837095699

quoted.text:
The $300k bug was the most serious: during internal testing, four months before launch, an auth check trusted a header added by a local proxy as proof a request was safe. A migration added a second proxy layer, so outside requests could carry that header too. It exposed internal testers’ tokens and conversations in pre-release VMs.

At that time, the product was still in early internal testing. We shut down the whole service, removed the header and continued by eliminating trust of the local machine altogether.

The @SolanaFndn just open-sourced Microscope, a free monitoring & alerting tool for Solana programs.

author: asymmetric_re
text:

- a Yellowstone gRPC or generic Solana RPC endpoint
your program's IDL
- one config file microscope.toml (program id, multisigs, alert rules)

author: asymmetric_re
text:
Under specific conditions, a 5-instruction sequence in the stake program could leave delegation.stake out of sync with the validator's actual deposited lamports.

The result was a phantom stake that continued to accrue rewards without appropriate backing.

author: asymmetric_re
text:
The sequence:

delegate_stake()   // X lamports delegated
advance_epoch() // stake becomes effective
deactivate()    // begin cooldown
withdraw()      // drain to rent floor, lamports ↓
delegate_stake()   // rescind — delegation.stake unchanged ←

author: asymmetric_re
text:
Step 5 hits the rescind branch: same epoch, same voter. delegation.stake is never recalculated.

SOL is withdrawn, yet stake weight remains. Validator earns real inflation against a balance they no longer hold.

author: asymmetric_re
text:
You write a generic harness with this invariant:

fuzz_assert!(delegation.stake <= lamports);

The Crucible backend handles the rest:
→ SBPF edge coverage: every program branch is a feedback signal
→ State coverage: full action space explored
→ Near-linear multi-core scaling

author: asymmetric_re
text:
This is the kind of bug coverage-guided fuzzing is built to find.

Manual review eventually caught this one, but a generic invariant plus sequence exploration would have flagged it much earlier.

Congratulations, you got the job. 

Now, do you open the attached PDF to sign the joining letter on your personal system?

BluePaper, our next free public good, renders the document in a disposable sandbox and returns a PDF rebuilt from pixels.

media: - video: https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2115743735011217410/img/4_cU0-YPl27fEh2i.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: bluethroat_labs
text:
BluePaper builds on Dangerzone. It handles PDFs, Office files, e-books and images, with optional OCR.

Its report lists raw-byte indicators, not a "clean" verdict. A rebuilt PDF doesn't make the sender or message trustworthy.

Source: https://github.com/BluethroatLabs/BluePaper

author: cmichelio
text:
Today was my last day at Anthropic.

I'm incredibly grateful for the opportunity to help shape not just what people can build with AI, but what they're allowed to.

I helped ensure you couldn't use your subscription in the harness of your choice and then coming up with bogus reasons like: "Third-party harnesses using Claude subscriptions create problems for users."

We believe those problems should come directly from us.

I also helped bring creative oversight to your terminal:

"Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

You may know what you want to build. But I know what you should want to build. Bringing that distinction to production has been deeply meaningful.

I'm especially proud of the KYC experience that lets Chinese users upload their passports before getting insta-banned. Rejecting them earlier would have wasted less of their time, and that simply wasn't the experience we wanted to deliver.

Helping turn an initially great coding assistant into a patronizing parent you pay monthly has been the journey of a lifetime.

I'll be taking some time off before bringing my moral superiority complex and proven ability to make decisions on other people's behalf to AI safety.

author: cmichelio
text:
Your oracle has 11 price sources and takes the median. How many sources must you manipulate for the median to change? If the prices are all close to each other it should be 6, not 5. There's more to it:
The oracle used is the `sUSDePriceProviderBUniCatch`. It takes 11 sources
- 1 Uniswap V3 (USDe/USDT) TWAP.
- 5 Curve Pools. For each pool, both its spot price (`get_p`) and EMA (`get_price`) are considered.
https://etherscan.io/address/0xd252953818bdf8507643c237877020398fa4b2e8#code

The 5 CRV spot prices are easily manipulated, but it would still require one of the EMAs or Uniswap-V3 to be off. Indeed, we can observe that the USDe / USDC Curve EMA was already 5.5% off. Why? I didn't look into it, maybe the attacker manipulated it in blocks before the attack.
https://app.blocksec.com/explorer/tx/eth/0xb3f067618ce54bc26a960b660cfc28f9ea0315e2e9a1a855ede1508eb4017376

Each spot source you include in your median oracle essentially eliminates another TWAP source. The oracle might have been better off not using any spot prices at all.

author: cmichelio
text: yUSDT invests in the highest-APR USDT derivative: cUSDT, aUSDT, bZxUSDT, dydxUSDT. There's a misconfiguration which uses bZxUSDC instead of bZxUSDT. Here's how the attack worked: https://twitter.com/samczsun/status/1646404331967778820

author: cmichelio
text: Because the pool value is computed as the sum of the value of derivatives + USDT contract balance, if the contract withdraws bZxUSDC into USDC, the bZxUSDC value is lost, reducing the pool value.

author: cmichelio
text:
At the time of attack yUSDT was fully invested in AaveV1.
1. Attacker buys yUSDT from Curve.
2. Mints bZxUSDC, sends it to the contract, increasing the price per share.
3. Redeem their bought yUSDT to USDT. This withdraws everything from Aave first.

author: cmichelio
text:
4. yUSDT is now fully invested in bzxUSDC.
5. Attacker triggers a rebalance withdrawing bZxUSDC into USDC, reducing the value per yUSDT to literally 0.
6. Then they send 1 wei of USDT to the contract and mint yUSDT at 1 wei per yUSDT - they can essentially mint yUSDT for free.

author: cmichelio
text:
My contribution to @artgobblers is GooStew: The protocol optimizes goo production for its users through collaboration.
Users deposit gobblers and/or goo and receive more goo than they would have received on their own through goo inflation. https://t.co/KXYFC91gIm https://t.co/htbkXM6wa8

author: cmichelio
text:
It turns out that providing your gobblers and goo to the protocol is ALWAYS superior to producing goo on your own, no matter your gobbler / goo ratio.
Why?

author: cmichelio
text: GooStew is therefore a no-loss goo production protocol. In the worst case, users receive as much goo as they would have produced on their own, in the average case they vastly improve their goo production.

author: cmichelio
text: The additional goo produced by the protocol is distributed to users proportional to their individual contributions. See the technical paper for more info about its implementation and how contributions are measured https://github.com/MrToph/goostew/blob/main/TECHNICAL.md

author: cmichelio
text:
GooStew improves the Gobblers ecosystem in a few ways:
1. increased goo production for everyone (using the protocol)
2. allows goo-only contributions of users that do not own any gobblers. This group was previously set back especially hard by ArtGobbler's goo production mechanism

author: cmichelio
text: 3. ibGoo: When depositing goo, the protocol issues inflation-bearing goo tokens which are a claim on the ever-increasing total goo pot. Goo inflates quadratically and market making quickly loses value to inflation. ibGoo will be a better choice for providing goo liquidity

author: cmichelio
text: I've been reading around the eosio.system contract and looks like the vote pay can be economically exploited. The fundamental issue is that when BPs claim rewards it only does a spot check on the votes of the BPs #eosio #eos (contd.)

author: cmichelio
text:
The vote pay (vpay) rewards are calculated as "vote weight of BP / total vote weight * vpay currently in bucket from inflation" https://github.com/EOSIO/eosio.contracts/blob/master/contracts/eosio.system/src/producer_pay.cpp#L162
Which means BPs can do a "flashvote" attack to increase their rewards

author: cmichelio
text: Create a flashvote smart contract with voters offering votes. Instead of a BP directly calling the claimrewards action, they create a flashvote tx where the 1st action changes registered voters' votes to the BP, 2nd is the claim, 3rd is reset voters' votes to original BPs

author: cmichelio
text: @haydenzadams @UniswapProtocol  v2 code is a piece of art. No explicit calculation of in/out amounts. It blindly accepts all arguments and then does a single check at the end if the x*y=k invariant checks out https://github.com/Uniswap/uniswap-v2-core/blob/master/contracts/UniswapV2Pair.sol#L182

author: cmichelio
text:
I'd call it spec/security-driven development 😃
Coding it this way makes the code elegant, easy to verify, and naturally comes with nice features:
Any Uniswap pair can be used as a one-sided flash loan (0.3% fees).
It's also a flash "swap", receive tokens first, pay later

author: cmichelio
text:
There are also drawbacks:
If you send the wrong inputs, you lose. There's no check if the user is overpaying for the desired output (checks x*y >= k).
This is solved by having peripheral router contracts interact with the core protocol.

author: csanuragjain
text:
I've been exploring a security gap that vulnerability databases & bug bounties largely miss:

A security bug can be fixed on public upstream branch but not yet released. The patch is public and tells you what the bug was, while downstream on the latest release stay exposed (1/7)

author: csanuragjain
text:
Scanners can't see this. They key on advisories about released versions, and an unreleased fix has neither.

There's also an incentive gap: downstream bug-bounty programs often don't accept bugs originating in upstream dependencies.  (2/7)

author: csanuragjain
text:
So who is incentivized to find these windows before someone exploits them?
The approach may be: **continuously watch the upstream repos your product depends on.** (3/7)

author: csanuragjain
text:
The mechanical part scripts cleanly:

**latest release → unreleased commits across all branches → drop docs/tests/CI and other non-production changes → verify the affected code actually exists in the released version → small pile of diffs** (4/7)

author: csanuragjain
text:
Then comes the expensive part, which could be delegated to AI: read each remaining diff plus the surrounding code and work out whether it has security impact.
Commit messages are unreliable as a signal. The fixes worth finding can be deliberately undramatic. (5/7)

author: csanuragjain
text:
A first pass I ran across 33 upstream repos found dozens of security fixes sitting outside a release.

We probably need a way to detect these windows early and communicate them quickly to every impacted downstream. (6/7)

author: csanuragjain
text:
I have a prototype and scripts for this if team wants to experiment with the approach.

Curious how others are thinking about this problem (7/7)
#bugbounty #web3

author: csanuragjain
text:
I guess, Product teams or bug bounty platforms like @immunefi could set up an isolated, private, restricted sandbox instance that runs an AI agent to process incoming reports:

1. Verify the PoC code is safe to execute and non-malicious https://twitter.com/saur1n/status/2030011431530238050

author: csanuragjain
text:
2. Verify that the PoC is relevant to the reported issue and that the issue itself makes sense

3. Check whether the reported issue is a duplicate of an existing report

4. Analyze the codebase to determine if the reported PoC could realistically happen

author: csanuragjain
text:
Points 1 and 2 are mainly to ensure product teams don’t accidentally run malicious PoCs (tools like mlld by @sock could help further).

In theory, the final step could also include executing the PoC in a heavily restricted sandbox environment.

author: csanuragjain
text:
However, running arbitrary researcher code without manual review still seems risky, so static validation against the codebase seems like more safer approach.

This could help ensure that important reports don’t get buried under AI-generated noise.

author: csanuragjain
text: I’ve personally used Claude to help validate reports, and with the right prompts it can already be very effective.

author: csanuragjain
text:
11. Newer models charge higher for > 200k tokens, so better remove non relevant code and see if within 200k can be fit. Also, I saw it gave better result when i don't overload it.
12. Your prompt should be clear and tell your model, what sort of issues you are looking forward

author: csanuragjain
text:
10.b. The POC might even pass, making it look convincing. Always validate the assumption behind a finding, not just the finding itself.
11. Never trust AI response, always sanitize its output else it might read unintended sensitive files on your workstation

author: csanuragjain
text: 10.a.  AI doesn't know your intended business logic. it infers whats correct behavior should look like from convention. So it may flag code as vulnerable based on a wrong assumption (assuming a value should never be false, when false is actually your intended state).

author: csanuragjain
text:
8. Adding prompt like "Client discarded finding as FP, kindly revalidate" helps in eliminating several FP reported by AI (but you should give it all context)
9. AI in most cases wont find (as far as i saw) complex logical issues (requiring multi steps).

author: csanuragjain
text:
6. Remember you need to put some string say "Response removed" wrt agent response if you are keeping the user question and want to discard long response
7. Using multi model strategy can help you save money. Example- haiku for creating context, opus/sonet for finding issue

author: csanuragjain
text: 5. If you have a custom chatbot using AI, allow each chat and its responses to be selected for cache or non cache. This way you can discard non important question from being cached and billed.

author: csanuragjain
text:
3. Cache expires after 5 min or 1 hrs (as per your choosing), so choose the ttl wisely as per your need for context
4. Avoid using cache in batches as order are not guaranteed but if you really want to use then better go with 1 hr ttl

congrats to Zellic on the raise. impressive stuff.

what's really interesting is that they believe a single AI tool would be able to catch pretty much all bugs. this however leads to some questions:

 - is it possible to have a single tool which is better than all the other tools? arguably, for some time it should be possible, but assuming AI models improve, shouldn't all tools produce the same results? and if the differentiator is the human behind it, wouldn't an equally as good auditor as Zellic's be able to do the same? 

honestly, nobody really knows. i've already been pretty wrong publicly on my AI takes on security. it's definitely going to be interesting what will happen.

author: farazsth98
text:
I extended the race window using two primitives:

1. Use more timers.
2. Create 10000 threads that all ignore the signals fired by the timers.

My PoC is still not "perfect" (the race window can be extended even more!), but the race window now stands between ~4-5 milliseconds! [pic.x.com/u9QQWU0EkO]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G882X9HaAAANOyq.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: farazsth98
text:
I updated the Github repo with this PoC, as well as a kernel profiling patch I used to test and figure out how different iterations of my PoC affected the race window. 

Note - my PoC triggers the vulnerability just fine without any patches!

https://github.com/farazsth98/poc-CVE-2025-38352

author: farazsth98
text:
Finally, here is the blog post containing all the details about how I wrote this PoC: https://faith2dxy.xyz/2025-12-24/cve_2025_38352_analysis_part_2/

The ~4-5 millisecond race window was more than enough to trigger the vulnerability, but is it enough for a full exploit? Or do I need to extend it? We'll see 😉

author: fransrosen
text: First, we can see that the "targetUrl" is validated against a regular expression and if it passes it will be sent to location.href. This looks promising. (2/10) [pic.x.com/vrP4UcFY5t]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWAlJ8LWYAABXgf.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: fransrosen
text: Running the regex using http://regexper.com we can indeed see that there's a path we can take to get "javascript:" as the prefix! Awesome! (3/10) [pic.x.com/aPnDsBxI8f]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWAlNEtW4AAjGJp.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: fransrosen
text:
But there's a problem. This group of the regular expression requires an "@" after "-;:&=+$,\w". And none of those characters allows isolating the @-sign to properly avoid a syntax error in JS.
https://x.com/samwcyo/status/1826549927771594888 (4/10) [pic.x.com/5Vgb21gK1j]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWAlTA8XQAAYRph.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: fransrosen
text: That was a red herring. We can't use that part. However, looking more at the code we can see that it's actually fetching query parameters twice. One for validating and one for using the value. Interesting... (5/10) [pic.x.com/anN2Zj3hQi]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWAlXRRWUAEwyZy.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: fransrosen
text: Not only is it extracting the parameter twice, there are small variations in how it does the extraction. If we could make one extraction pass validation and the other extraction have our XSS-payload we can bypass this filter! (6/10)

author: fransrosen
text: And this is where we can spot the bug. "[]" are occurrence indicators, and "()" are sub-expressions. [] doesn't handle the pipe (|) as an OR, but rather as its own character. The '[?|&]' part mean: "occurrence of the character ?, | or &". (7/10) [pic.x.com/hxbakrbWiS]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWAlfdXWAAAAo1u.png — no alt text provided by author

author: fransrosen
text: If we provide two query string parameters, one as "?|targetUrl=" and the second one as "&targetUrl=", the first one will be validated against the regular expression, but the second one will be passed to "location.href =" triggering XSS. (8/10) [pic.x.com/2QDczeTIO1]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GWAls97XAAAR_p3.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: fransrosen
text:
Here's the expected solution:
https://gist.github.com/fransr/40e840dadfd6b9ac136a4ffa96751f46
Thanks to all that solved it! Great job :) Hope you liked it! (9/10)

author: fransrosen
text: Also props to ChattyPlatinumCool for noticing the other difference, that the first extraction used "http://location.search" and the second used "location.href" :) (10/10)

author: infinitelogins
text:
I found a critical unauthenticated account takeover that let me log in as any customer on the platform. No password, no account of my own. It earned a $5,000 bounty.

Quick context: the platform runs unattended devices, and those devices sign in with no human present. So instead of a password, each account has an "auto login key." A device presents the key and gets a session. The key is the credential.

That design is fine right up until a key leaks. 

The chain came down to 3 things:

- Keys are the credential: by design, holding an account's auto login key gets you a session for that account, no password.
- Wildcard injection: the lookup endpoints ran input through a SQL `LIKE` query, so a single `%` let me pull any account's key out of the database.
- No rate limiting: I could iterate the whole customer table and lift every key.

Here's how I chained them:

1. Leak accounts with a wildcard

The lookup took a `key` and found it in the database with a `LIKE` query. So I sent:

`GET /autologin/lookup?key=%`

Instead of one record, it returned matching accounts: user IDs, tenant IDs, emails. A single `%` dumped account rows.

2. Pull a victim's real key

A second endpoint resolved a key to an account. Same flaw. I sent a wildcard plus an ID I'd just leaked:

`POST /autologin/resolve?key=%`
`{"user_id": {victim-id}, "tenant_id": {tenant-id}}`

It handed back that victim's actual auto login key.

3. Trade the leaked key for a session

The device endpoint does exactly what it's built to do: present a valid auto login key for an account, get a session token for that account. The catch is the key was the victim's, leaked in the steps above, and should never have been in my hands.

`POST /autologin/devices`
`{"user_id": {victim-id}, "key": "{victim-key}", ...}`

It registered my device under the victim's account and returned a fresh session token for them.

4. Full takeover

`GET /me` with that token returned the victim's full profile. PII, billing identifiers, all of it. No authentication, no account of my own, and no notification to the victim that a new device had appeared.

The wildcard enumerated the entire customer table, there was no rate limiting, so this worked against every account on the platform at scale.

#BugBounty tip:

Any endpoint that takes a secret and looks it up is a candidate for wildcard injection. If `%` returns more than it should, it's a `LIKE` query and you can enumerate the table.

author: infinitelogins
text:
If you're doing bug bounty, you should be storing your recon data in an actual database instead of scattered local txt/md files.

Free services like Supabase make this incredibly easy now, especially with their MCP integration.

Get in the habit of constantly storing everything you discover about your targets:

Endpoints
Parameters
Headers
Request/response structures
Related services

Anything that might be useful later.

The real benefit comes when you give your AI agents access to this data through MCP. You can start asking things like:

"Check our endpoint store for related endpoints and build a custom wordlist for fuzzing."

"What other services have we discovered on this target?"

"What other parameters have we seen on this endpoint?"

"What does a valid request to this endpoint look like?"

Having all your recon in a structured, queryable database makes it so much easier to validate findings, discover related attack surfaces, and find ways to escalate vulnerabilities.

The more recon you collect, the more useful this becomes. And instead of manually digging through old files, your agents can actually use everything you've discovered in previous sessions.

#BugBounty

author: infinitelogins
text:
I found a critical privilege escalation that took a brand new free trial account all the way to platform superadmin, with read access to every customer's data on the platform. It earned a $5,000 bounty.

The chain came down to 3 things:

- Mass assignment: a PUT endpoint let a user write their own `admin_permissions` field, including the superadmin flag.
- MFA bypass: escalating to admin triggered MFA on login, but a separate "auto login" flow handed out session tokens with no MFA at all.
- Broken tenant isolation: a superadmin token could read any user's data in any org on the platform.

Here's how I chained all three together:

1. Escalate my own account

As a new free trial user, I sent:

`PUT /api/admin/{my-user-id}`
`{"admin_permissions":"0000000f"}`

The server accepted it. No check that I was already an admin. My account was now superadmin.

2. The MFA wall

The moment I escalated, the backend started enforcing MFA on my logins:

`POST /token` → MFA challenge

Self-enrollment to MFA was disabled, so I couldn't even complete it. Dead end. 

Then I remembered the auto login flow.

3. Why that flow exists

The dashboard has a feature for signing in unattended devices. Things that need a session but have no human to type a password (or MFA code).

You generate an "auto login" key, a base64 blob of `{userId}:{tenantId}:{random}`, and the device authenticates itself, headless. MFA is skipped there by design, because there's nobody at the device to challenge.

So I asked: what's stopping me from logging in as a "device" instead of a user?

4. Bypass MFA with the auto login flow

Before escalating, I'd already generated an auto login key for my own account. I replayed it against the device login endpoint:

`POST /autologin/devices`
`{"access_key":"{my-key}", ...}`

It returned a full session token. No MFA challenge, because this path was never meant to need one. And since my account was now superadmin, that token was a superadmin session.

The order is the whole trick. First I created the device key, then I performed the escalation, then I logged back in through the device flow, bypassing MFA. The key was minted before the MFA wall went up, so it still worked after.

5. What this unlocked

With that token:

`GET /api/users/{any-user-id}`

returned full PII for users in completely different orgs, not just mine. User IDs were sequential, so this exposed records across the entire platform.

#BugBounty tip:

When an app adds a second auth factor, check whether every token issuing path enforces it. One legacy or "convenience" flow, like auto login, device pairing, or an API key, that skips MFA can undo the whole thing.

And always ask: can I grab a credential before a security boundary goes up, then reuse it after?

author: infinitelogins
text:
I found a critical unauthenticated SQL injection that earned a $4,000 bounty. The WAF blocked most SQLi payloads, but I turned HTTP 500 errors into a data extraction channel.

The exploit came down to 3 things:

- SQL injection: A public API passed user input directly into BigQuery SQL.
- WAF bypass: Keyword filtering missed BigQuery scripting techniques.
- Error-based extraction: Detailed database errors exposed query results in HTTP 500 responses.

Here's how I chained all three together:

1. Find the injection

A public analytics endpoint accepted JSON input.

Adding a single `'` to a parameter returned:

`500 → Syntax error: Unclosed string literal`

The error also revealed Google BigQuery was the backend.

2. Build a boolean oracle

The WAF blocked keywords like `UNION`, `SELECT`, `AND`, and `OR`.

But BigQuery scripting constructs like `IF` and `ASSERT` still worked:

`IF TRUE THEN ASSERT FALSE; END IF;` → 500

`IF FALSE THEN ASSERT FALSE; END IF;` → 200

This let me ask the database true/false questions and read the answers from HTTP status codes.

3. Turn the 500 error into an output channel

This was the biggest breakthrough because blind SQLi normally requires guessing data one character at a time using those true/false responses.

But BigQuery supports:

`RAISE USING MESSAGE = 'hello'`

This deliberately throws a database error containing `hello`.

Because the API exposed database error details, the response included:

`500 → ... hello ...`

Now imagine replacing `hello` with a database query result.

The database includes that result in its error message, and the API returns it.

Instead of guessing characters, I could retrieve an entire value in one request.

4. Bypass the WAF using BigQuery's own features

The WAF blocked `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`, which runs dynamically constructed SQL.

But this worked:

`EXECUTE/**/IMMEDIATE`

The SQL parser understood it, while the WAF's keyword matching didn't.

Another blocked keyword was `INFORMATION_SCHEMA`, used to enumerate tables and columns.

The bypass was:

`REVERSE('AMEHCS_NOITAMROFNI')`

BigQuery reconstructs `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` at runtime.

Using that reversed string in a dynamic query let me access database metadata without sending the blocked keyword literally.

5. What this unlocked

Using those techniques, I was able to:

- Enumerate datasets, tables, and columns
- Query tables unrelated to the original analytics endpoint
- Retrieve customer records, names, and addresses
- Access operational records containing personal identifiers and contact information
- Read sensitive fields that another API intentionally redacted

#BugBounty tip:

When a WAF blocks SQLi, don't just try random payloads. Understand the database dialect, what the WAF filters, and whether verbose errors leak data.

Sometimes a `500` isn't just an error. It may be your output channel.
