quoted.text: @saxenism @TeeDotFail If the attacker can run a node, TEEs are useless. And if you dont let people run nodes in blockchains, they can’t independently verify the state. Hence there is no configuration in which you can both prevent an attacker from being root on his own machine and have public

author: saxenism
text:
1)
Before we discuss the usefulness of TEEs, here are a few ground realities that we should align on:
+ ORAM makes this attack infeasible**
+ The researchers did NOT extract the attestation keys from every TEE.
- For AMD SEV-SNP, they only recovered application-level keys

author: saxenism
text:
2)
- For Nvidia's GPU CC, a forged TDX attestation is a prerequisite for their attack.
+ To be able to pull this attack off in the real world is exponentially harder and costlier
+  TEE exploits are localised. A compromised node CANNOT compromise other nodes over the network.

author: saxenism
text:
3)
+ TEEs have already been widely in use for years by major firms with real regulatory risks outside our web3 industry. So security maturity of TEEs >> other privacy tools.
+ There is absolutely no restriction on using TEEs as a complement to rest of the privacy techniques.

author: saxenism
text:
4)
TEEs are not a silver bullet.

I never claimed them to be one and NO tech should be considered that.

TEEs should be run with layers of defense around it & in conjunction with other privacy-preserving techniques, such as ZK or MPC based on the criticality of the task at hand.

author: saxenism
text:
5)
A TEE is an interesting piece of technology, with its own set of security guarantees under a given threat model.
It is important to identify the true nature of TEEs and understand its true essence to be able to efficiently use it in web3 protocols.

author: saxenism
text:
6)
Problem Statement:  Exploring can TEEs be used to provide privacy to users in a permissionless chain?

Immediate Problem: For any public blockchain, public verifiability is a MUST. By default, the nodes of this TEE blockchain network will be processing the transactions...

author: saxenism
text:
7)
via the blockchain VM inside TEEs which will encrypt everything by default. Hence none of these network nodes can share data of these txns with a full node so that anyone who run a full node can replay all transactions and be assured of the correctness of the blockchain state

author: saxenism
text:
8)
Proposed Solution:

• TEE attestations for privacy
• ZK proofs (arguments of knowledge) for verifiability
• Governance for security edge cases not handled by the above combination

author: saxenism
text:
9)
1. ZK Proofs (arguments of knowledge) serve two main purposes:
- Introduces verifiability in the network
- The main issue with “TeeDotFail breaking TEEs” is that TEEs can basically attest to anything and thereby include invalid transactions in the blocks.

author: saxenism
text:
10)
-- Well, if the node can produce the attestation for a particular block but is unable to produce the ZK Proof for that block, then that is a pretty good indicator that a particular TEE node has been compromised.

author: saxenism
text:
11)
-- Anyone can verify the state of the blockchain based on the info posted by the node, ie, initial state, ZK proof of state transition and final state.

2. Would chain performance deteriorate since nodes would have to process transactions inside TEEs & generate proofs too?

author: saxenism
text:
12)
Not really.
For a given node, “completing the job” would entail the following:
+ Process the transactions, build block and broadcast the proposed block + Provide the attestation to the proposed block
+ The block is optimistically considered valid

author: saxenism
text:
13)
+ Some other node takes up the work for proposing the next block
+ Now the original node has to generate ZK proof of the validity of the proposed block
+ Next the node will deliver the ZK proof of the block and the attestation of running the proving correctly

author: saxenism
text:
14)
+ Node can generate small ZK proofs that do not require a lot of computational power
+ A separate external aggregator can aggregate them into a larger one.
+ Aggregating does not require witnesses

author: saxenism
text:
15)
+ Assuming ALL credentials provided by the TEE node (ZK proof and both attestations) check out, the block is finalised
+ If ANY of the provided credentials fails the checks, the node is considered to be compromised and is kicked out of the network or penalised or whatever.

author: saxenism
text:
16)
This approach preserves the performance of the network along with the security guarantees with the worst case being a rollback.

3. How do we handle the worst-case scenarios?

There would be a few more edge cases even with this ZK-TEE model, assuming a compromised TEE node.

author: saxenism
text:
17)
There would be cases like:

+ We lose MEV protection when a compromised node build a block
+ Privacy breaches: Compromised nodes can generate valid attestations and ZK proofs, but if they have compromised their TEE, they can leak sensitive data.

author: saxenism
text:
18)
+ Force rollbacks/DoS: Attackers can refuse to post valid proofs, or post conflicting proofs under different branches, forcing rollbacks, forks, etc.

To handle the cases where the malicious behaviours cannot be attested on-chain, we will rely on governance + PoA consensus

author: saxenism
text:
19)
Why governance?

The core committee of the blockchain, or basically anyone, should be able to create a proposal for malicious behaviour by a particular node, get it voted on and remove/penalise such nodes from the network.

author: saxenism
text:
20)
Why PoA?

Use consensus mechanisms such as Proof of Authority where the operators are known & have massive reputational and legal risk. With PoA it is easier to require multi-cloud diversity, audits, and immediate revocation on compromise.

author: saxenism
text:
21)
Obviously, strict standards of operational security & hygiene go without saying and to contain the blast radius of a TEE compromise, avoid storing secrets as much as you can in TEEs & use rapid key rotation & short-lived delegation window to reduce the window of exploitation

author: saxenism
text:
23)
With our current security model this edge-case will be extremely hard to detect since with this theft the compromised node will still be able to produce correct attestations and ZK proofs.

So, we introduce the following enhancements to our network architecture:

author: saxenism
text:
24)
+ Switch to remote signing in the HSM/KMS. This way, enclaves get no long-lived keys.
- TEEs only get access to ephemeral keys.
- Security policies for any signing: rate limits, time-locks, circuit breakers, etc
- Fast rotation + revocation to reject stale quotes

author: saxenism
text:
25)

+ Break down the single entity of our “blockchain nodes” into multiple actors:
- Sequencer nodes → They sequence encrypted transactions into a block. Since the transactions are encrypted, the sequencer CANNOT engage in MEV & censorship. Since the sequencer does not need to

author: saxenism
text:
26)
- Executor nodes → The only entity that needs to run inside of the TEE. It decrypts the sequencer’s batch commitment + ciphertexts inside TEE, run the VM, produce (A→B) ZK proof, and a TEE quote for the execution binary/config.

author: saxenism
text:
27)
- Signer(s) / Finaliser → sign the block/proof tuple. Enforce policy checks (rate limits, value caps, allow/deny lists, timelocks). Long-lived protocol keys live in HSMs/MPC, not in executors. Each signer exposes an operator identity attestation (PoA) and maintains a

author: saxenism
text:
29)
5. So, what would now be the worst-case scenario when keys are leaked with our current architecture? 

Even if the executor TEE were compromised and its ephemeral decryption or application-level keys were leaked, it still cannot alter the blockchain’s global state or inject

author: saxenism
text:
30)
+ Execution correctness is verified independently via ZK proofs. Any deviation from the expected state transition invalidates the proof.
+ Block validity requires signs from separate signer nodes, whose long-lived ECDSA keys reside in external HSMs/MPC, not in the TEE.

author: saxenism
text:
31)
+ Attestation identity of the executor is tied to its enclave measurement. A compromised enclave identity can be immediately revoked from the registry, cutting off its ability to decrypt new txns or have its proofs accepted.

author: saxenism
text:
33)
- Even with an ephemeral key leak, the only realistic impact is temporary loss of confidentiality for that block’s transactions. 
-  The attacker could decrypt that batch’s ciphertexts and see plaintext transactions
- But they cannot:

author: saxenism
text:
34)
-- Reorder transactions (ordering is sequencer-determined and zk-verified)
-- Alter execution (ZK proof fails if even a single opcode or state delta mismatches)
-- Persist their access (ephemeral key expires post-block)

author: saxenism
text:
35)
-- Re-sign or replay the block (final signature keys live in HSM/MPC, outside the TEE)

So, while the theft of application-level keys may theoretically expose a narrow window of privacy leakage, it does not compromise network integrity, verifiability, or consensus.

author: saxenism
text:
36)
The combination of ZK proofs, externalised signing, and attested ephemeral key lifecycles effectively neutralises the attack vector in real-world deployments.

As a further defense, when signing or proving for sensitive operations, we can also employ MPC:

author: saxenism
text:
37)
Instead of a single TEE producing proofs, require “m-of-n independent provers” across clouds/providers/regions to jointly produce/endorse a block proof

author: saxenism
text:
38)
So, back to @randhindi's original point... no, TEEs are NOT useless in permissionless networks, when combined with ZK and incentive-based governance. This TEE-first privacy network is permissionless yet has verifiable privacy.

author: saxenism
saxenism

quoted.text:

ORAM does make the @TeeDotFail attack obsolete, but there is subtlety.

TeeDotFail relied on deterministic encryption of addresses and creating a reliable ciphertext pattern dictionary out of that for the exploit.

Had ORAM been active https://twitter.com/msakiart/status/1984727295773364722

author: saxenism
text:
@randhindi 40)
TEEs aren't dead. 
TEEs are maturing, arguably faster than any other tech out there.

If we can just give up our childish stubbornness to dunk on TEEs only tech and tell how it doesn't fit into web3 like a glove... we can have a very powerful primitive at our disposal.

author: saxenism
text:
32)
+ Sequencers see only ciphertexts & cannot reorder or censor selectively without collusion. Since they never see plaintext, MEV opportunities are minimised by design.
+ Ephemeral key rotation ensures that a key leak is only valid for a single block & cannot be reused.

author: saxenism
text:
28)
- Prover/Aggregator (optional) → aggregate/recursively compress the many small proofs from executors.

author: saxenism
text:
22)
4. What about the case of: Theft of application level keys

In the @TeeDotFail paper, the researchers were able to extract application-level keys from AMD SEV-SNP. They extracted the ECDSA private key used by the OpenSSL library to sign messages.

author: saxenism
text:
The @TeeDotFail research broke the confidentiality & integrity guarantees of TEEs & that’s huge.

But the way it’s being presented feels more like a hit-piece than an honest discussion.

Let’s unpack this attack & I'll tell you why it makes me more bullish on TEEs, not less 👇🧵 https://twitter.com/yrschrade/status/1983273836326834233

quoted.text:
🚨 TEEs are AGAIN compromised! 🚨

This time it's even bigger!

TL;DR
-  3 weeks ago: Intel SGX exploit (DDR4)
-  Today: Exploit affecting the latest State-Of-The-Art TEEs by Intel, AMD and Nvidia (DDR5)

TEEs don't bring privacy or security in crypto.

All you need to know 👇🧵 https://t.co/J0S0zXJBxU

author: saxenism
text:
2) Let's handle all claims from this post one by one.

> Whoever has physical access can exfiltrate data, assets and even break verifiability.

No.
For this attack, the attacker not only needs to have physical access, they need to be root as well. [pic.x.com/S7RGTBahbX]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G5EfSxtbIAMagY0.png — no alt text provided by author

author: saxenism
text:
3) Now,  what does root mean?

Physical root -> attacker needs to be able to do whatever they want with the TEE, including physically plug/unplug DIMMs, add interposers, attach probes, access on-site serial console, force reboots or BIOS changes and whatnot.

author: saxenism
text: 4) Software root -> attacker should be able to do whatever they want with the TEE's software, such as the ability to flush caches, pin virtual pages to specific physical frames, manipulate page tables, load/unload kernel modules

author: saxenism
text:
5) This is the PRE-REQUISITES for this attack.

You literally need to put a physical interposer between the DIMM & DIMM slot.

AND

lower the memory rate to 3200 MT/s

AND

software access to force cache flushes, page pinning, etc etc

and, this is JUST THE SETUP for the attack.

author: saxenism
text:
6)  > Researchers have shown using TEEs for blockchain & distributed AI applications is fundamentally flawed

No. That is your independent inference.

Researchers showed that given physical access & root(h/w + software), the security guarantees of TEEs can be broken. That's it.

author: saxenism
text:

For AMD SEV-SNP (with ciphertext hiding) -> Researchers extracted the OpenSSL ECDSA signing keys and NOT the AMD attestation/platform keys(application-level keys and not system-level keys) [pic.x.com/SL8qjPs45C]

author: saxenism
text: 9) For Nvidia's GPU CC -> A forged TDX attestation is a PRE-REQUISITE for this attack. The attack on Nvidia's solution in the paper is an attestation relay attack. [pic.x.com/R6sGPWNJfc]

author: saxenism
text:

But grouping other TEEs in the same sweep misdirects people into thinking that every TEE out there had its PCK extracted.

author: saxenism
text:
11) Next, the team broke:
> secure block building with TEEs
> privacy-preserving AI (training & inferencing)
> being front-run by the operator of a TEE DEX

This is entirely true. If you extract the attestation keys of a TEE then it has been stripped away of ALL it's power.

author: saxenism
text: 12) Post-acquiring the PCK (without detection), you can quite literally do anything with a TEE (or whatever's left of it). It's up to your imagination and resourcefulness as to what kind of hiests you can pull off. [pic.x.com/Ngk688YbTA]

author: saxenism
text:
13) So, are TEEs a singular point of failure in protocols and shouldn't be used?

Well, the real question is, do we understand TEE well enough to create safe protocols with it? Here are two aspects to this:

a) Central points of failure in general
b) Protocol design with TEEs

author: saxenism
text:
DeFi protocols rely on oracles, entire L2s run with a single sequencer, and on and on and on.

So, a centralised point of failure is NOT something that we are new to.

15) Protocol Design w/ TEEs

Should we simply ignore the centralisation risks of TEEs?

Absolutely no.

author: saxenism
text:
16) To safely use TEEs, we have to upgrade our understanding of the actual security guarantees of a TEE, improve our threat models and overall design resilient protocols.

We have to write enclave-grade code: constant time crypto code, and avoid predictibility at all costs.

author: saxenism
text:
17) Want a concrete example?

Sure.

The biggest limitation of a h/w attack like the (@TeeDotFail) attack is that they are localised. Typically, h/w attacks only affect a single machine at a time in a single geographical location.

author: saxenism
text: 18) So, it would make sense for your protocol to have an m-of-n TEE threshold signing architecture for critical operations across enclaves in regions around the globe, ideally with independent providers (remember the recent AWS outage)

author: saxenism
text:

> Anyone can perform this kind of attack with cheap, hobbyist level equipment. The full setup costs below $1000

author: saxenism
text:

author: saxenism

author: saxenism
text: 29) But even if we assume that everything goes through, as soon as this attack gets mounted and they do even one reboot (which is mentioned in the paper), the applications running on that server will be migrated to another instance.

author: saxenism
text:
30) So, anyone would have a VERY HARD time compromising a real application(on serverless deployment)_ with this attack, even with all things going right for them.

Basically, with this level of modification, no application will keep running on a given server.

author: saxenism
text:
31) Also in most cloud/production TEE deployments: cloud tenants have neither h/w nor software root.

DC staff may have physical access but not isolated software root on target VMs.

This dual-requirement significantly narrows the threat model in practice in my opinion.

author: saxenism
text:
Yes. For that, we really need to drill down into constant-time coding practices.

What that means is implementing cryptographic code so that execution time, memory access and control flow DO NOT depend on secret data.

Eg,
+ No branching like `if(keybit == 1) { ... } else { ... }
+ No array lookups indexed by secret values
+ All operations (multiplication, XOR, modular exponentiation, etc) take identical time and touch identical memory addresses for all possible secrets.

All this would typically imply giving up on a few optimisation tricks, but it's all about how much hindrance you can add in the path of a really motivated adversary.

quoted.text:
Fucking Hell. I kinda understand now why judging and triaging sucks for everyone involved.

I don't have time. The triager doesn't have time. The client doesn't have time. Everyone's BP is going up.

How to solve this mess?

1. triager & whitehat get on a video call.
2. call is time-bound. 30 minutes tops.
3. a mutually chosen upon LLM, pre-fed with all required context joins.
4. LLM listens to entire conversation and the pleas made to the LLM specifically from both parties.
5. whoever LLM thinks is right at end of 30 minutes, is the winner

===

Irrespective of the outcome:

If the judge was right and wins: the drama doesn't drag on.
If the judge was right and loses, the client simply doesn't implement the fix

If the whitehat was right and loses: he just reports it after the contest in a BBP.
If the whitehat was right and wins: he makes bank

The Math:
An extractor sees an opportunity worth k. We add an app-level tax T(x) = τx on top of their priority fee x.

Their profit-maximizing bid becomes x_* = k/(1+τ).

The key takeaway: the dApp now captures a  τ/(1+τ) share of the MEV pie.

author: saxenism
text:
A rather elaborate hack/drain attempt on me

I want to share a story with everyone, especially my security researcher friends, about an age-old scam going on, but in a new skin.

So, here's what happened.

1. I announce that I have left ZKSync's security team in a tweet that garners a bunch of attention online.

2. A bunch of people follow me from that tweet, including this person, @Zixi_Eth (img0)

3. 2 days later, I receive a text from him stating that @mirana is looking for a security expert to help them with their security requirements and sends a pretty detailed message about the responsibilities (img1)

4. I pick a date and time from Zixi's Calendly. Check out @mirana's actual teams page and DO FIND a Zixi Wang listed there (img2). Since it did not have a "Twitter", I grew a bit sus of this account.

5. The time for our meet comes. I hop over into a Zoom call, he takes a full-fledged interview and asked questions like:
a) Most exciting bug you ever found
b) Hardest challenge you solved at your workplace
c) What inspires you 
YADAYADAYADA

6. Then he proceeds to drop THE line that makes every rational decision-making drop dead in its tracks. He said that, according to him, I am the PERFECT FIT for the role, and the pay would be a minimum of $250/hour.
a) This is a classic rugpull move, where the scammer tries to heighten an emotion (greed, in this case) to make you underthink your next decisions.

7. He says, "yk what, actually our CEO's on a call right now with the `core operational team`, how about you jump on the call now, and we can finalise your contract today itself.
a) ANOTHER red flag: "Rushing me"

8. So, he sends over an invite link to a workspace at jandi[dot]ai. Says it's a Slack alternative popular in China. 

> I am almost out at this point in time, but just play along to see where the actual scam happens.
> Specifically, the link was: jandi[dot]ai/invite/workspace-2M3QOL

9. So, I sign into the new work with an email id which was (unfortunately) not a burner email. And I see a meeting happening there, but the bummer is I CANNOT join the meeting on my browser.

> A pop-up claimed that I HAD to install a Mac/Windows client to access this "feature". This was followed by the "Download Now" link ofc.

10. Zixi, my saviour, texts me on Jandi, asking if something's wrong and offers to help me "set up Jandi" over a Zoom call.

11. I ask him to kindly fuck off, but he still says, "Don't worry, I'll invite my CEO over a Zoom call if you're not comfortable with Jandi and share your assessment with him in the meantime".

12. I disconnect and reach out to legitimate employees at @mirana, and they confirm that this handle is, in fact, an imposter (img3)

====

That's it.

That's the story.

Read it, learn from it and stay safe.

The only reason I am sharing it here on X is that I was able to protect myself this time because I had read about multiple drain (attempt) incidents from a LOT of CT folks. 

They helped me build my invariants for interacting with strangers from CT. 

Huge shout-out to everyone who shared their learnings with the world even after losing money and powering through the embarrassment. You are THE BEST.

Thanks.

author: saxenism
text:
The stakes in blockchain are different. A bug doesn't just mean downtime - it could mean irreversible financial losses. 

We need to balance transparency with security.

Open source remains crucial for trust and innovation, but it needs to be deliberate, not immediate.

author: saxenism
text:
Instead, foundations/companies should set clear timelines for open-sourcing different components of their codebase. 

Before the public release, the code should have had multiple professional audits, thorough internal reviews, and rigorous PR review processes.

author: saxenism
text:
Core blockchain infrastructure powering our industry should absolutely be open sourced. 

But timing matters. 

"Building in public" should NOT be our default. 

Open sourcing shit as you code it, is probably not the best decision as well.

author: saxenism
text:
While Linus's Law ("given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow") helped scale Linux, the blockchain industry needs a more nuanced approach. 

We're not just dealing with software crashes - we're dealing with millions in potential losses.

We all need to take a moment and give our appreciation to the pioneers of decentralized security audits. I personally owe much of my success to the opportunities they've created. In the face of competition it continued to stay faithful to its policies and treated researchers fairly, even if it meant losing business.

It is true that in recent times C4 has become a shadow of what it once was, for various reasons. But I'll remember them for the epic competitions, intellectual judgment discussions and friends made on the way.

On the business side, this is part of the phase-out of crowd audits, which are no longer feasible to run with AI submissions. For years the gig has stopped being profitable and used for customer acquisition and upsell potential, but now it's official. Security is already converging to multiple AI passes followed by A-tier team audit(s) for finding outliers, and a bounty program as last defense. 

So-long C4. You will be missed. 🐺

author: trust__90
text:
The ironic thing is that this will sound to many like old people come across when irrationally fearing technology. But this time the "technophobes" are right, and it's just a matter of how many AI catastrophes need to happen until the rest understand it.

Here's the core truth accelerationists don't want people to understand: every non-AI process running on your computer can, with some amount of effort, be explained by a computer scientist. Once AI is involved, the "why" something works is gone, and all you're left with is a pattern of processing that seems right on the surface. But without understanding the piping, by definition you cannot make any positive statement about its correctness.

Any time humans or computers act based on LLM output it carries an unbounded leak risk. To be clear this is not going away in the next Claude or ChatGPT release, it's completely structural and baked into the tech. Every user needs to decide whether the risk/reward tradeoff is worth it. The problem starts when (a) users are kept blind about these risks and (b) powerful players make the opt-in decision for everyone.

That is not to say that LLMs are not incredibly useful. Unfortunately (not particularly smart) people keep equating the arguments "LLMs are unreliable" and "LLMs are useless", this way they can cancel you and lets them keep chasing unrealistic world views. 

I seriously hope I'm wrong about this, but we're going to see more and more "rm -rf /" tier screw ups in the coming years. Anyone reading tech news is already seeing this acceleration. But what's even more worrying than the computational leak is the human processing leak. What happens when elections are decided based on wrong, or manipulated premises? Can't say I'm waiting to found out. Humanity had an arguably good thing going before this, it's too bad financial greed (stock has to go up right?) is going to send us crashing into walls without as much as a seat belt.

quoted.author: lonelysloth_sec
quoted.text:
Giving LLMs permissions outside a completely contained sandbox was always a bad idea -- and will keep being a bad idea.

If you wan to let those things act without asking for confirmation all the time (and the default  should  be not wanting it) you need to start by defining exactly what it can be allowed to do, in the most restrictive way possible. Ideally not even a command line -- it can call a few scripts that do very limited things, and you heavily scrutinize those scripts.

Treat LLMs as adversaries bc they will try to replicate whatever behavior they learned from the internet and RLHF and who knows what sort of thing that means. 

Sysadmins would never give any new human hire the sort of permissions to do that. But apparently LLMs are now God so we need to trust them with everything.

text:
CT focusing on the low-hanging fruit takes -
"How could KelpDAO be this negligent to configure 1/1 DVN?"
"Why is LZ supporting such unsafe config?"
"How did AAVE risk management team not flag this setup?"

While valid, these are the wrong questions to be asking. 

As an industry after each exploit we always seem to point fingers at the most easy to blame component, pretending we'd be fine if only "X wasn't this stupid". I read this as a psychological coping mechanism designed to sidestep the existential question - can we ever truly achieve the required level of security guarantees to replace TradFi?

Vanilla crypto usage (e.g. BTC, ETH transfers) is generally as secure as the weakest link between cryptographic attacks, key safety, and consensus layer. This is a fairly formal mathematical surface. Then contracts were introduced, each one creating a new, unique attack surface. It wasn't good enough apparently. We decided the contracts should be arbitrarily changed at runtime, so now every company sporadically calls people together to sign bytes they don't understand, but the Safe UI says are safe. But we were too greedy to call it a day, so we devised protocols that secure billions of dollars using hot wallets (AKA bridges). Automated infrastructure operating off of RPC calls to route billions of dollars. 

What we've ended up with in the de-facto state of DeFi is a system of software and network layer trust assumptions similar or inferior to TradFi, without benefiting from its defensive mechanisms - transaction voiding, regulatory compliance, legal accountability, money trail etc. In other words, the on-chain aspects are a distraction for a traditional, completely trusted setup without all its upside.

We need the collective narrative to finally accept the fact that threat actors have an arsenal of 0days which they weaponize to get access to highly privileged systems. With AI assisted/automated exploitation patch gapping 1days has also become a central threat. The fact we don't see 9-fig exploits every day (although it feels so lately) is not because our security is airtight, but due to operational capacity and prioritizing highest EV ops. 

The security endgame questions every corp needs to answer are: How many unique exploits or supply chain attacks are needed to compromise critical assets? How do we implement security barriers that cannot be bypassed by device compromise? For example, the security guarantees of a 3/7 MS of top hardware wallets is drastically different from compromising an RPC endpoint. On-chain time locks and volume thresholds add another friction point to bypass and drastically reduce worst case scenarios unless another bypass is chained. 

Would a 2/2 DVN setup have made a big difference? I don't know. LZ likely has much greater resources and depth to secure a validator than smaller orgs, and evidently was still compromised. What's almost certain though is that when, not if, 2/2s will get compromised, we'll just see the industry continue moving the goal posts, to cope with security nihilism which has only one (taboo) conclusion: TradFi is far superior than the current mess we call DeFi.

Until we come back to effectively paper-wallet security, we'll continue to witness ever more sophisticated software exploits tarnishing whatever is left of user trust. And if we can't reach that level of confidence while providing a competitive service to TradFi, then I rather we go to zero on our own terms, rather than sent to zero by DPRK hackers.

quoted.text:
Looks like there is a USDC bridge possible exploit on Arbitrum!

@blockaid_ detected an abnormal bridge withdrawal that extracted ~$24.15M USDC from an Arbitrum USDC custody bridge contract. The on-chain bridge logic was not bypassed; the malicious withdrawal was authorized by a quorum of hot-validator signatures and then finalized after the dispute period.

Exploit tx: https://arbiscan.io/tx/0x50d0b3ec6c3f5fce0f10abf81540bbb508f421494aa2b3480c4a264b0436547b 

Root cause: compromise or abuse of the bridge's hot-validator signing path. Five hot-validator signatures authorized a withdrawal of 24,150,000 USDC to the loot wallet, reaching 7,142 / 10,000 validator power (>2/3 quorum). The bridge contract then treated the withdrawal as valid and released funds after the 200-second dispute period.

The attacker subsequently bridged/laundered the proceeds to Ethereum: the same loot wallet received ~24.146M USDC minted on Ethereum in batches and forwarded the funds onward, consistent with movement of the stolen Arbitrum USDC.

Found a cool bug today, thought i should share it.

I was looking at the oauth flow, when i realized that there was a clientid that i didnt recognize, it was different from the clientid of the web app...

(a thread)

author: xssdoctor
text: After some digging, i realized that this was the oauth flow for the iphone app. The flow went like this. the iphone app would redirect to safari. The user would log in on safari, and the redirecturi would redirect back to the app via a deeplink

author: xssdoctor
text: well it turns out that I could set any protocol in the redirecturi. The purpose of this is because ios allows custom protocols for deeplinks. So i made a malicious iphone app which redirects into safari with the callbackuri pointing to my malicious app, it leaks the token to my backend. The backend immediately does the token exchange. ATO!

text:
window.opener is special. it is a way for one window/tab to reference another and persists across redirects.

As opposed to x = http://window.open("second.html") that will NOT persist if the window is redirected.

author: xssdoctor
text: the problem with http://window.open is that it only goes one way. The opened window can reference the opener with http://window.open but the opener cant reference the opened window

author: xssdoctor
text: Another important thing to remember is that you can only open a window or tab with user interaction. The exception to this rule is if you are opening a window into an ALREADY opened window/tab

author: xssdoctor
text: this is where http://window.name comes in. if you have a window that has a name (http://window.name = "booyakasha"). another window/tab in the same tab group can open a window WiTHOUT user interaction with http://window.open("second.html", "booyakasha")

author: xssdoctor
text: putting these things together, we can see that if the first window declares a http://window.name and then the opened window immediately opens a window with http://window.name() using the http://window.name of the first window, you now have 2 windows that can

author: xssdoctor
text: There are MANY use cases for this. this helps with postmessage exploits (now both windows can send postmessages to each other even if the pages are redirected multiple times), self-xss etc

text: try it yourself. it feels like magic.

text: I've been working on a very cool xss chain today with @HackingNotes (a thread)

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes So http://target.com has a self-xss, but it requires a LOT of user interaction (3-4 clicks). This would be exploitable if chained with clickjacking

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes most of the pages are not frameable, but we find one that is http://target.com/frameable page. HOWEVER, when you frame the page, you lose all cookies and the framed page is logged out and redirects to /login

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes HOWEVER. the parent pages are STILL logged into the attacker account. this is actually a fantastic scenario. If we can get xss on this frame, we can achieve xss on the parent (victim) page

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes While there were a number of login csrf's for this target, none were frameable. we COULD however, log in to our accounts in the frame using a third party oauth provider. if we could get the victim to click the "login with [redacted]" the frame would be logged in as the attacker

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes So using some help from our boy @Mokusou4, we found a login csrf for the oauth provider

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes @Mokusou4 So here is the attack scenario. attacker page 1 has a script which has http://window.name = "booya". then upon button click, it opens up attacker page 2 THEN redirects itself to the oauth login csrf. Then page 2 does http://window.open("victim page", "booya").

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes @Mokusou4 THIS will open that FIRST page to our victim page, and allows us to access it through window.opener. Now on attacker page 2. we frame "https://target.com/frameablepage" and use clickjacking to have the victim click the oauth button

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes @Mokusou4 now the frame is logged in as the attacker. Now we do some more clickjacking to trigger the xss. The xss payload is <img src=x onerror="alert('window.parent.opener.document.cookie')">

author: xssdoctor
text: @HackingNotes @Mokusou4 this works because the cookie was NOT httponly. We now have the auth cookie to the victim's account and have ATO

text: Just found an extremely cool bug. I was looking at the main page of my target. I noticed that there was a third party iframe that appeared for about 2 seconds while the page was loading. I found the origin and found reflected xss. The problem was that I had a 2 second window to

author: xssdoctor
text: So ordinarily in these situations, the attack works like this: you open your http://site.com/firstpage.html. This page opens http://vulnerablethirdpartysite.com. Then you redirect the initial page to http://victim.com, which has the vulnerable iframe on it.

author: xssdoctor
text:
The reason behind this is that window.opener is magic. It’s basically the only way to see into the frames of another page, as long as the frames are same origin. 

So window.opener.frames[0].location.href = “JavaScript:alert()”

author: xssdoctor
text: The problem here is that the iframe was ephemeral. So not only did I have to do the above, but it had to be exploited as a race condition

author: xssdoctor
text: Also, the frame was in a different  numbered frame each time the page was opened. Sometimes it was frames[15] and other times it was frames[20]. So what I did was open page A to my first attacker page. The user clicks a button which opens the third party which had my xss

author: xssdoctor
xssdoctor
text: This code sets an interval of 10 milliseconds and continually looks at all of the frames and sees if it can read location.href of any of them, if so, it redirects to JavaScript:alert(). The xss will fire every time.

author: xssdoctor
text: While this is extremely cool, I do not expect a big payout. There was. I postmessage gadget so all I have is xss within the iframe which is in a different origin than my main site. Still it was really fun to exploit. Shout out to @Rhynorater for his “open faced iframe sandwich”

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
New https://zk.golf challenge ⛳️ Google ID Token Claims Extraction.

Take the raw JSON payload of a Google ID token, parse it, check it against Google's schema, and extract the claim values. All inside a circuit. (1/8) [pic.x.com/0BStN6wHnc]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVdxRE6WIAAPFzs.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
Parsing JSON is a fundamental primitive for verifying JWTs in zk circuits.
Checking the signature isn't enough: the circuit has to extract the values it cares about (iss, aud, email, exp…) so that it can enforce properties on them. (2/8)

author: zksecurityXYZ
text: JSON parsing in a circuit has always been hard. The circuit has to handle a lot of variation: extra fields it doesn't expect, nested objects, escapes, and keys that can appear in any order. (3/8)

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
A lot of existing circuits take shortcuts: "it's signed, so it must look the way Google writes it", and they skip full JSON parsing.
A common trick is substring extraction: find the key, then read up to the next quote. (4/8)

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
This challenge takes no shortcuts.
The circuit gets the raw bytes and must accept exactly the valid tokens. Every accepted input must be:
- a valid JSON document
- matching the ID token schema we defined in the spec
- with each extracted key appearing at most once in the document (5/8)

author: zksecurityXYZ
text: Here’s an example extraction. The set of claims to extract is fixed: for each schema key present in the input document, the “presence” flag is set to 1 and the value is extracted. Missing keys get a 0 flag and zeroed slots, and any extra keys in the document are ignored. (6/8) [pic.x.com/GUFtM77fWT]
media: - photo: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVdyAolWgAATazx.jpg — no alt text provided by author

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
The best part: we never wrote the circuit ourselves.
We wrote the specification: a reference JSON parser and a simple declarative schema of what an acceptable Google ID token looks like. A few days later, an agent had written the corresponding circuit. (7/8)

For the ZK crowd: circuits unroll the rounds, so constraint count is linear in rounds.

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
Why it's fine here: the best known collision attack on Keccak reaches 6 rounds.

Twelve is double that. Keccak has more third-party cryptanalysis than any of its peers, and 6 rounds is as far as anyone has gotten.

To score a circuit we ran it on one fixed input, `default` and we checked correctness on a a symbolic all-variable input; so it is correct for every input.

So cost was looking at one input and correctness/completeness at every input. 

That's the bug in essence.

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
It works because of one asymmetry: 
The specs can be simple but the circuits implementing them can be complex. LLMs are happy to do the boring work of proving that the circuit matches the spec. Humans only need to read the spec.
Sometimes you can trust the magic talking box!

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
How we got here: we wrote a Lean spec for SHA-256. 
Then we asked an LLM to write an optimized circuit.

The result was the most efficient SHA-256 compression in R1CS by a wide margin.
We never reviewed the circuit, it literally cannot be broken.

We call it fearless optimization

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
The first two known exploits against live ZK circuits just happened, and they weren't subtle underconstrained bugs. 

They were Groth16 verifiers deployed without completing the trusted setup ceremony. One was  white-hat rescued for ~$1.5M, the other drained for 5 ETH.  

🧵

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
Both protocols used Circom + snarkjs, the most common stack for Groth16 deployments. 

The bug? They skipped Phase 2 of the trusted setup: the circuit-specific contribution step.

Without it, the verification key's γ and δ parameters are both set to the same value: the G2 gens

author: zksecurityXYZ
text: The scary part: this wasn't a deep cryptographic flaw or a subtle circuit bug. It was a deployment mistake: missing one CLI command. And it sat in production with real funds at risk.

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
takeaways:
- Always review deployment scripts, not just circuit code
- Check your verification keys: if vk_gamma_2 == vk_delta_2, your proofs are forgeable
- We worked with @DedaubSecurity to scan EVM chains for other affected contracts, no high-value ones found, but some exist

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
We've also added detection for this class of vulnerability to zkao, our AI-powered continuous security scanner for ZK circuits. A missing Phase 2 contribution is exactly the kind of deployment-level issue that benefits from automated checks.

full post: https://blog.zksecurity.xyz/posts/groth16-setup-exploit/

AI vulnerability research is non-deterministic.

The same model looking at the same code won't take the same reasoning path every time. Some paths find nothing. Some paths find the bug.

Introducing zkao. [pic.x.com/9KwUw3gpIn]

author: zksecurityXYZ
zksecurityXYZ
text:
zkao makes AI security research work the way fuzzing works: not as a one-shot event, but as something you run continuously until coverage compounds.

We're starting with Circom, where we have deep expertise from 100+ ZK system audits.

author: zksecurityXYZ
text:
Your coverage improves along three axes:

1. models get better
2. our patterns get richer (learned from real Circom audits)
3. probability compounds with repeated runs

Even if your code doesn't change, your security coverage does.

author: zseano
text: Did a bit of hacking past few days and I still prefer manual hacking over relying on AI. Even for writing reports. Manual hacking is just so fun (time consuming tho..) and gets my brain working. And when I find a bug I feel like *i* have achieved it. Not AI.. “found a bug!”🙄

author: zseano
text:
Plus when it comes to writing reports I like to do a “mental dump” on what I found, impact, and how to reproduce it yourself. No waffle, no bs.. just straight up facts for the team to read and understand. 

AI generated reports give me a headache😅
